title: U.S. and Saudi Arabia strike "Iran-aligned terrorists" in Iraq
summary: The U.S. and Saudi militaries announced airstrikes late Tuesday on Iranian-backed groups in Iraq, after Iran and its proxies allegedly targeted American forces.
story: The U.S. and Saudi militaries launched airstrikes late Tuesday on Iranian-backed groups in Iraq, U.S. Central Command said, after Iran and its proxies allegedly targeted American forces over the last few days.

The strikes could pose a challenge to a five-day lull in U.S. attacks on Iran, as President Trump says he wants to give diplomacy a chance. It's unclear when — or whether — strikes on Iran could resume. The U.S. also said Tuesday it prevented an Iranian "surprise attack."

The U.S.-Saudi operation was aimed at "terrorist logistics and weapons sites across eastern Iraq," CENTCOM said in a statement posted to social media. The Saudi Ministry of Defense also confirmed that it "conducted precise and targeted strikes," citing its right to self-defense.

The Popular Mobilisation Forces (PMF), an Iraqi paramilitary group backed by Iran, said at least 20 of its fighters were killed and 32 wounded in a statement released Wednesday. The group said its headquarters in Baghdad and six other locations were struck.

CENTCOM said the strikes were in response to more than 30 attempted drone attacks on U.S. forces and Saudi energy sites over the last three days, describing the attacks on U.S. assets as unsuccessful. Saudi Arabia said it has intercepted drones that were launched from Iraq and targeted petroleum facilities in Riyadh and the country's east.

The two countries did not name the groups in question, but Iran backs several Shiite militia groups in Iraq that have launched rockets at U.S. forces in the past. Some, like Kata'ib Hezbollah, are designated by the U.S. as foreign terrorist organizations.
CENTCOM alleged the attacks were directed by Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps.
"The IRGC and its terrorist proxies must cease these attacks to avoid further U.S. military response," CENTCOM wrote in its statement.
Earlier Tuesday, CENTCOM said Iran's Revolutionary Guards mounted an "attempted surprise attack," launching ballistic missiles at U.S. forces in the region. The missiles were intercepted.
The scattered attacks come as the U.S. holds off on directly striking Iran, after carrying out almost two weeks of nightly strikes on Iranian targets that ended Thursday night.

Mr. Trump said Tuesday morning that the U.S. and Iran have had "very good talks," expressing optimism that the two countries could reach an agreement, but he warned that the U.S. will "finish the job" if a deal isn't struck with the Iranian regime.

Iran has said it isn't currently seeking direct talks with the United States. Sticking points between the two countries remain, including over Iran's push to maintain control over the Strait of Hormuz and the U.S.' desire for Iran to give up its uranium enrichment program.

Meanwhile, another Iran-backed militant group — the Houthis in Yemen — has fired at Saudi tankers in the Red Sea, threatening a key waterway off Saudi Arabia's western coast as Iranian attacks seal off the Strait of Hormuz on the other side of the Arabian Peninsula.

title: Japan quake kills at least 13; more trapped in collapsed mall, factory
summary: A major earthquake in Japan's southwest killed at least 13 people and left several injured or missing after a shopping center and a paper mill were heavily damaged.
story: Soldiers and emergency workers combed through a badly damaged shopping mall, paper mill and collapsed houses looking for trapped survivors Wednesday after a powerful earthquake that killed at least 13 people and left many missing in southwestern Japan.

Bullet train services and some airport operations remained suspended and damage was still being assessed a day after the magnitude 7.1 earthquake struck the Kumamoto area on the southern main island of Kyushu.
"There are people who are still waiting to be rescued, and it's a race against time," Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi said. "We will go all out to find and rescue as many people as we can."
About 36,900 homes were still without electricity, 9,500 homes were without gas and communication networks were not working in some areas, chief government spokesman Minoru Kihara told reporters.

More than 9,000 people left their homes to stay in more than 500 shelters, and he said power sources were being added so the evacuation centers had air conditioning. Japan has had an ongoing heat wave, and temperatures in the area were forecast to exceed 90 degrees Fahrenheit as a heat wave hitting the nation continued.

Public broadcaster NHK reported Tuesday that two victims were women in their 20s who were confirmed dead in a heavily damaged Aeon Mall shopping center in the city of Kashima in Kumamoto Prefecture. A third person was also found without vital signs, NHK said. The local fire department said that the second floor of the mall had collapsed.
NHK said the mall collapse followed an explosion that was likely caused by a gas leak.
Police in the city earlier told CBS News' Japanese partner network TBS that there were "a lot of deaths" in the mall, but that it would "take time to confirm the exact number."

There were at least 11 people trapped inside the Nippon Paper Industries Yatsushiro Plant in Kumamoto after a chimney collapsed during the quake, according to TBS, and two of them were later found without vital signs.

The quake that struck at 4:27 p.m. local time (2:27 a.m. ET) had a magnitude of 7.1, according to the Japan Meteorological Agency, but reached the highest possible level of 7 on Japan's Shindo scale of shaking. The U.S. Geological Survey measured the quake — one of hundreds that strike Japan every year — at 6.8. The vast majority cause little damage.
At least 50 people were taken to hospitals and local emergency services and at least six other people were rescued earlier, according to NHK. Their conditions were unknown.
Takaichi said on social media she had established an emergency operations center.

"I extend my heartfelt condolences to all those affected by the disaster," Takaichi said. "The government will work tirelessly through the night to swiftly assess the overall damage situation and carry out emergency disaster response measures, starting with the rescue and lifesaving of those affected."
Video aired by NHK showed several blazes, damaged bridges, a derailed cargo train and cracked roads after the temblor struck at the far southern end of Japan's main Kyushu island.
The Japan Meteorological Agency initially issued an alert for a possible tsunami of up to 3 feet, but withdrew the warning after a couple of hours.
No immediate abnormalities were recorded at nuclear power plants, the Nuclear Regulation Authority said.

Toyota said Wednesday it would halt operations at three plants in southern Japan through Friday, a mere  hours after resuming operations it had stopped on Tuesday, so it could assess the temblor's impact on suppliers and logistics, the Reuters news agency reported. And Honda said it would keep its Kumamoto motorcycle plant idle until Friday so quake-damaged parts of the factory can be repaired.
Kumamoto was hit by two devastating earthquakes in 2016 — one of magnitude 6.5, followed two days later by one of magnitude 7.3 — which killed 273 people and injured more than 2,800.
A quake with a magnitude of 7.2 hit northern Japan on June 25 but caused no deaths or major damage.
Japan is one of the world's most seismically active countries, sitting on top of four major tectonic plates along the western edge of the Pacific "Ring of Fire."

The archipelago, home to around 125 million people, typically experiences hundreds of jolts every year and accounts for about 18% of the world's earthquakes. The vast majority are mild, although the damage they cause varies according to their location and the depth below the Earth's surface at which they strike.
Japan is haunted by the memory of a massive 9.0-magnitude undersea quake in 2011, which triggered a tsunami that killed or left missing around 18,500 people and wrecked the Fukushima nuclear plant.
A tremor measuring 7.7 hit the country's north on April 20 this year, injuring at least 10 people and shaking large buildings in Tokyo.
That prompted authorities to issue a special advisory warning of an increased risk of earthquakes of magnitude 8.0 or stronger.
The advisory was lifted after a week.

title: Trump meets with Zelenskyy and Netanyahu amid wars in Iran, Ukraine
summary: President Trump met with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu Tuesday.
story: Washington — President Trump met with both Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu separately at the White House Tuesday amid the war with Iran and Russia's invasion of Ukraine.

Neither meeting was open to reporters. Zelenskyy and Netanyahu attended the funeral of Sen. Lindsey Graham, a staunch supporter of both Ukraine and Israel. Graham had just returned from a trip to Ukraine before his sudden death at 71. His last public words were in Kyiv.
Mr. Trump later posted photos from both meetings to his Truth Social platform. On his meeting with Netanyahu, the president described it as "very good."
"Obviously, many important subjects were discussed," Mr. Trump said, but did not elaborate.
Mr. Trump said his meeting with Zelenskyy "went very well," also writing that "many things were discussed."

Zelenskyy earlier said his meeting with Mr. Trump was "good" and that they discussed the licenses for the production of Patriot missile interceptors, critical in Ukraine's efforts to combat Moscow. Mr. Trump and Zelenskyy most recently met earlier this month on the sidelines of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization in Turkey, where Mr. Trump announced the U.S. would allow Ukraine to build its own Patriot missiles.

"A good meeting with President Trump at the Oval Office," Zelenskyy wrote on X. "Thank you for everything we do together to protect the lives of Ukrainians and advance peace. First and foremost, I offered President Trump our condolences on the passing of Lindsey Graham. He was a true friend of Ukraine.

"The president and I discussed licenses for Patriot interceptor production and several other ideas that could help. We also spoke about diplomacy – it's important that the diplomatic process be reinvigorated. Our teams will arrange the details of their further communication. I am grateful to the United States for its firm support."

Immediately following the Zelenskyy meeting, Mr. Trump met with Netanyahu behind closed doors. Neither the White House nor the Israelis have yet released a readout of that meeting. It was their first known face-to-face meeting since the U.S. and Israel launched the war with Iran.

Mr. Trump, who has typically been one of Netanyahu's staunchest supporters, has put distance between himself and the Israeli prime minister of late. Although he's called Netanyahu a good wartime president, Mr. Trump hasn't said whether Netanyahu should continue as prime minister in the future. Netanyahu, Mr. Trump has said, needs to apply a "softer touch" and "be more responsible with respect to Lebanon."

In an interview with Fox News Tuesday morning, Mr. Trump pushed back when he was asked about reports that Netanyahu planned to discuss information related to Pickaxe Mountain in Iran, an underground nuclear site. Mr. Trump said he doesn't need someone else to tell him what's happening there.
"I don't need Bibi to tell me that," Mr. Trump responded, adding that Netanyahu is "telling me that because he wants me to stay involved."

title: Friend describes last known movements of missing American in Grenada
summary: American Elizabeth Waddell was last seen on July 22 while visiting the tiny Caribbean island of Grenada.
story: A friend of the American woman who went missing while vacationing on the Caribbean island of Grenada said there is video that shows her last known movements. Police have since confirmed that surveillance footage captured Elizabeth Waddell the day she was last seen, July 22, swimming off Grand Anse Beach in Grenada's capital city, St. George's.
Her friend, Amanda Romano-Harmon, described it as showing Waddell "floating" and "swimming around."
"But then she, you know, she floats out of the camera view and so that's the last footage of Liz," Romano-Harmon said.

Video showed the 44-year-old North Carolina mom walking toward a pier along the beach at around 11:30 a.m. that morning, said Royal Grenada Police Acting Commissioner Randy Connaught at a Tuesday briefing. Over the next 30 minutes or so, it showed her sitting on the sand nearby, walking on the pier, entering the water, and, finally, swimming beneath the pier just after 12 p.m., Connaught said.
About 45 minutes later, Waddell's friend and travel companion was seen walking toward the pier, but she later returned alone, according to the acting commissioner.

"Mrs. Waddell was not seen returning from the water," Connaught said. He added that investigators have received eyewitness accounts that indicated she had been swimming in the open ocean later in the afternoon, not long before Waddell's friend reported her missing to police.

Police have not publicly released the surveillance footage or images related to Waddell's disappearance, but the family on Tuesday released some of the footage themselves. Wadell's husband, Cailen Waddell, said in a statement earlier Tuesday, before they released the video, that the family had reviewed the footage themselves after traveling to Grenada to help with the search.

"I went out and did this swim yesterday," he said, referencing the path his wife appeared to take. "It is easy. There are lots of rocks you can stop at if you need. The water is shallower near shore, where Liz could touch if she wanted."
Cailen Waddell said police were working on connecting with the eyewitnesses who reported interacting with his wife farther from shore at around 5:30 p.m. on the day of her disappearance.

"I understand that there are likely many questions, and there are for me too," he said. "I am heartbroken that she is missing. Those of you who knew us best knew our commitment to each other, to travel, to nature, and exploring the world as a team."

Waddell was on a three-week vacation with her close friend Heather. According to the family, Waddell left their Airbnb around noon. When she didn't return for hours, the family said Heather went looking for Waddell and found her towel, but no other signs of her.

"Liz had literally left in a swimsuit with a towel. She didn't have her phone, ID, anything with her, no shoes," said Romano-Harmon, who described the beloved physical therapist as "the type of person who'd give you the shirt off her back."
Waddell's husband has described her as "a loving free-spirit person," telling Grenadian media last week that his wife "could make friends with anyone and she often did."

Police are asking boaters and residents in the area for anything they may have seen regarding Waddell. They're also working to collect more security footage from hotels along the beach, according to her husband. Connaught said search efforts have so far covered land and sea.
The State Department is aware of the reports of a missing American in Grenada, a spokesperson said.

title: Kenya investigates deaths of 15 elephants in Amboseli National Park
summary: The Kenya Wildlife Service said 10 of the elephants showed signs of partial paralysis before dying within two days.
story: The deaths of 15 elephants over the past month in Kenya's Amboseli National Park have sparked an investigation, wildlife officials said Tuesday.

The Kenya Wildlife Service said 10 of the pachyderms showed signs of partial paralysis before dying within two days, while the remaining five were found dead, with their carcasses partially consumed by scavengers.

Most of those affected were female elephants and their calves, with only one male among the dead. The deaths happened in the Kimana Sanctuary and Kuku Ranch areas surrounding the park, the authority said.

Kenya has previously recorded incidents of elephants being poisoned as a result of poaching and human-wildlife conflict. But officials say it's the first time in decades the region has recorded elephant deaths on this scale, according to CBS News' partner network BBC News.
KWS said there was currently no evidence pointing to a single cause of death, BBC News reported.

Preliminary tests on samples collected from the elephants by a laboratory at the University of Nairobi detected a "potential toxic substance," while separate analyses by Kenya's Government Chemist were negative for the toxins tested. KWS said further tests are underway.

"Environmental investigations are also being undertaken, including the analysis of water sources and other potential environmental contaminants within the affected areas, to establish whether the elephants were exposed to a common source," KWS said in a statement.
Officials sought to reassure the public, saying there was no evidence the condition could be transmitted to humans.

The Amboseli National Park is located near the Tanzania border at the northwestern foot of Mount Kilimanjaro. There were more than 2,000 elephants in the Amboseli ecosystem as of 2025, according to BBC News.

title: Woman murdered in 1936 and buried under building is finally identified
summary: Police have finally identified the remains of a woman murdered nearly a century ago and buried beneath a building in Toronto.
story: The remains of a woman murdered nearly a century ago and buried beneath a building have finally been identified thanks to modern forensic testing.
The woman was identified as Mary McLeod Moffat (née Davidson), a Scottish national who immigrated to Canada with her family in 1913, according to police and the laboratory that performed the testing.
The culmination of the case brings closure to "one of Toronto's oldest mysteries," detective Michael Kelly, of the Toronto Police Service, told Canadian news site CTV News Toronto on Monday.

The case couldn't have been solved without investigative genetic genealogy, a technique that uses advanced DNA profiling to build a "family tree" that can eventually help identify an unknown individual, said Kelly.

Although police believe the woman's murder took place around April 1936, her remains weren't discovered until May 18, 1995, when workers uncovered them at a demolition site in Toronto, according to the Toronto Police Service. At the time, forensic exams determined that the woman was "intentionally buried," after being struck at least six times with "a hammer-like weapon," police said.

A homicide investigation was opened to learn more about what may have happened to her, but collecting a suitable DNA sample from the remains was difficult because so much time had passed and their condition deteriorated.

Police began to review the case in 2022, submitting new DNA samples for testing to a lab that specializes in investigative genetic genealogy and unsolved murder cases. Scientists faced substantial challenges as they attempted to recover "only small amounts of severely-degraded human DNA" from the remains, but they did ultimately collect enough to build a forensic profile, according to the lab.

After generating leads and, subsequently, a follow-up investigation, investigators were able to find Moffat's relatives, collect DNA samples from them and compare those samples to the ones pulled from her remains, which allowed them to identify her.

Investigators later determined Moffatt's husband, Andrew Lloyd Moffat, likely killed her. After his wife's death, he went on to live in Vancouver and the United States under the alias Drake Lloyd Cummings, police said. He died in 1985.

Moffatt's case was one of two longstanding unsolved murders in Toronto that have now been closed because of investigative genetic genealogy, police said. The second identified the badly burned remains of a woman who died in the passenger's seat of a vehicle that went up in flames on April 22, 2004, after intentionally crashing into a tractor-trailer. Her name was Patsy Flora Lagarde.

"These identifications represent the significant impact that investigative genetic genealogy can have on long-term unidentified human remains investigations," said homicide detective Stephen Smith, of the Toronto Police Force's missing persons and cold case unit, in a statement. "After decades without answers, we have been able to restore the identities of Mary Davidson and Patsy Lagarde, provide information to their families, and uncover important facts about the circumstances surrounding their deaths."

title: Widow of murdered mayor arrested in extortion case in Mexico
summary: Valentin Lavin, who was allied with President Claudia Sheinbaum's leftist party, was shot and killed during a town hall.
story: Mexican authorities on Monday arrested the widow of a mayor in central Mexico who was shot and killed last week, on charges she was involved in an extortion case, according to prosecutors and local media.
Valentin Lavin, the mayor of the town of Temoac and allied with President Claudia Sheinbaum's leftist party, was shot and killed during a town hall on July 22.
The crime occurred in the state of Morelos, a region close to Mexico City where several drug cartels are active.

The state prosecutor's office said Monday they arrested Marisol "N," which the Mexican press identified as the mayor's widow, as well as Geovany Emmanuel "N," chief of the municipal police. The office released images of both suspects with their eyes blurred out, as is customary in Mexico.
Prosecutors said both were detained as part of an anti-extortion operation, though it did not provide further details of the arrests or if it had any connection to Lavin's death.

Almost 100 mayors have been murdered in Mexico since 2006, when drug-related violence surged, official figures show. Since the current government took office in October 2024, at least 14 mayors have been murdered in the country, Uno TV reported last week.

Earlier this month, attackers shot dead the husband of a Mexican councilwoman, with the gunfire also injuring the politician and her daughter as the family was reportedly on their way to a school graduation.
The country was particularly shocked by the fatal shooting of mayor Carlos Manzo in the state of Michoacan last November, during Day of the Dead celebrations.
Sheinbaum said July 14 that homicides in Mexico had  fallen by nearly half since September 2024, touting the reduction as a result of her security policies since taking office.

story: Dan Wakeford, founder of Celebrity Intelligence, discusses Prince Harry's expected UK return, his relationship with King Charles, and why a meeting with Prince William remains unlikely.

"William loves his father and appreciates better than anyone how underestimated Charles has been over the years. He wants the king to leave his mark on history. But deep down, he knows he and his family — particularly his wife, Kate — are the future of the monarchy."

Prince William, Prince of Wales, meets young people and volunteers in the Common Room at Eagle House on July 9, 2026, in Hastings, England. (WPA Pool/Getty Images)

"King Charles is tired," Andersen stressed to Fox News Digital. "He would like to have everything as it was before Megxit. But he knows how willful William is. Queen Elizabeth's cousin Margaret Rhodes told me more than once that the relationship between Charles and his late mother wasn't cozy. But what people don't know is that the royal family isn't set up to be 'cozy.' Well, it still isn't. It's 'The Firm,' remember?"

Prince William, Prince of Wales and King Charles III walk behind Queen Elizabeth II's coffin as it is transported on a gun carriage from Buckingham Palace to Westminster Hall ahead of her lying in state on Sept. 14, 2022, in London. People magazine reported Harry is expected to visit his home country again in September. The Sun also reported that the king plans to offer him a room at Buckingham Palace in London for his stay. Royal broadcaster Ian Pelham Turner told Fox News Digital that Charles' reported offer to accommodate Harry in September is "a potential lifeline" that also sends a message of "defiance" to William, who reportedly wants "no further contact with his estranged brother."

Prince Harry, Duke of Sussex departs from The Invictus Games Foundation Conversation: From Policy to Practice at Chatham House on July 7, 2026, in London. Multiple royal experts told Fox News Digital that there's no doubt King Charles' younger son misses his life in the U.K. (Eamonn M. McCormack/Getty Images)
British broadcaster and photographer Helena Chard told Fox News Digital that William is known for being stubborn behind palace doors and is not one to forgive easily.

Prince William (pictured here) did not meet with his estranged younger brother, Prince Harry, who spent time with their father, King Charles III, at Highgrove House, the monarch's private residence, on July 10, 2026. (Chris Jackson/Getty Images)
"Megxit forced William to grow up fast as the future king," she said.

From what I understand, he felt his father didn't handle that firmly enough. He also believes in protecting it by drawing hard lines. But he's not the king yet."

Prince William, Prince of Wales, known as the Duke of Rothesay and Catherine, Princess of Wales, known as the Duchess of Rothesay when in Scotland, smile to well-wishers as they arrive for a visit to Aros Hall, a local community hub on April 29, 2025, in Tobermory, Scotland. Since marrying in 2018 and making their royal exit in 2020, the Duke and Duchess of Sussex have been attempting to carve out their own independent roles outside the monarchy. (Joshua Sammer/Getty Images)

Prince William, Prince of Wales and Prince Harry, Duke of Sussex attend the Committal Service for Queen Elizabeth II at St. George's Chapel, Windsor Castle on Sept. 19, 2022, in Windsor, England. (Getty Images)

Kate Middleton kisses Prince William as she presents the prizes after the DMI Royal Charity Polo Cup 2026. (Max Mumby/Indigo/Getty Images)

title: Anthony Fauci's Hollywood supporters: Julia Roberts, Katy Perry and Orlando Bloom among celebrity backers
summary: From Julia Roberts' "personal hero" to Katy Perry and Orlando Bloom's "Fauci Gang," Hollywood's biggest stars rallied behind Dr. Anthony Fauci during COVID-19.
story: Laura Ingraham and Raymond Arroyo examine newly released diary entries from Dr. Anthony Fauci, highlighting his fascination with Hollywood and celebrity culture. The entries detail Fauci's interactions with celebrities like Julia Roberts and Barbra Streisand.
Julia Roberts, Katy Perry and Orlando Bloom were among Dr. Anthony Fauci's biggest celebrity supporters during the height of the COVID-19 pandemic.

As the 85-year-old infectious disease expert became the face of America's COVID-19 response after the pandemic became a global crisis in March 2020, he also attracted an unlikely fan club in Hollywood – including Brad Pitt portraying him on "Saturday Night Live at Home."

While chronicling his management of the spiraling health emergency, Fauci also wrote frequently of his rapidly rising fame in his private 2020 journals, which were released by Senate Homeland Security Committee Chairman Rand Paul, R-Ky, earlier this week.
FAUCI'S NEWLY RELEASED COVID DIARIES REVEAL BIZARRE FIXATION ON FAME AS PANDEMIC DEATHS MOUNTED
"The situation with my national and international fame is explosive and really unimaginable," Fauci wrote in a May 21, 2020, entry in his diary.

Julia Roberts, Katy Perry and Orlando Bloom were among the stars who lined up behind Dr. Anthony Fauci during the COVID-19 pandemic. (William B. Plowman/NBC via Getty Images; Kevin Mazur/Getty Images; Taylor Hill/FilmMagic)
"It is not hyoperbole [sic] to say that today I am the most famous and talked about person in the country and one of the most recognizable peson [sic] in the world," he added.
Fauci also dedicated significant space across numerous entries to logging his personal interactions with Hollywood A-listers, including Julia Roberts, Barbra Streisand and Sean Penn among others.
Fauci's personal journals were released ahead of his scheduled testimony before the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee. (Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images)
INSIDE FAUCI'S PRIVATE DIARY: WHAT HE WROTE ABOUT TRUMP, TV PERSONALITIES AND CELEBRITIES

As Fauci comes under increasing scrutiny ahead of his scheduled testimony before the Senate Homeland Security Committee as part of its investigation into the origins of the pandemic, here's a look at the celebrities who publicly championed the longtime public health official during the pandemic.
Julia Roberts
Julia Roberts gushed that Fauci was her "personal hero." (Amy Sussman/Getty Images)
Julia Roberts raved over Fauci while conducting an Instagram Live interview with him as part of ONE Campaign’s new #PassTheMic series.
"How rad that we have maybe the coolest man on the planet right now," the Oscar winner told viewers before Fauci joined her on the video call. "Wow, this is intense."
Roberts then gasped and beamed when Fauci appeared on the screen, saying, "Oh, this is such a thrill."

"This is a thrill for me because there are very few experts of anything in the world, and you truly have emerged as a personal hero for me," she added. "Just to have this little corner of your time for us is such a joy."

In a May 2020 diary entry, Fauci wrote about his "wonderful discussion" with Roberts, who he described as "absolutely fabulous" and "totally down to earth." He also shared that he was "embarrassed" when she told him that he was her personal hero.

On Feb. 10, 2021, Fauci detailed how Roberts presented him with amfAR's Award of Courage virtually from her home in California. "When my image came up on the screen she gasped and said that every time she sees me her throat gets dry and she gets nervous and excused herself to go into the kitchen and get a glass of water," he wrote.
Kim Kardashian
Kim Kardashian organized a Zoom call with Fauci and 36 other celebrities. (Taylor Hill/Getty Images)

In April 2020, Kim Kardashian organized a private Zoom call with Fauci which included 36 other celebrities, athletes and influencers. Katy Perry, Orlando Bloom, Gwyneth Paltrow, Ashton Kutcher, Mila Kunis, Brad Falchuk, Tiffany Haddish, 2 Chainz and Dennis Quaid were among the notable attendees.

"It was a whole bunch of movie stars and some sports figures, and they wanted to know about what they could do to stay safe, about wearing masks and avoiding crowds," Fauci said of the hourlong call in a November 2020 interview with CNN. "I was impressed by the questions they asked, by their level of sophistication."
EXPOSED FAUCI DIARY SHOWS HE ESTIMATED COVID-19 DEATH RATE TO BE MUCH LOWER THAN WHAT HE TOLD CONGRESS
Fauci explained that he agreed to the call due to the group's enormous reach, noting that they had "megaphones" and "could get the word out about staying safe."

"Each of them has enormous numbers of followers on their social media accounts," he told CNN. "I could say to them, for example, it's important to wear a mask, and they get on their accounts and say 'wear a mask' and it goes out to an additional couple of million people."
Katy Perry and Orlando Bloom
Katy Perry and Orlando Bloom wore "Fauci Gang" hoodies. (Stefanie Keenan/Getty Images for Academy Museum of Motion Pictures)

Katy Perry and Orlando Bloom, who were engaged at the time, actively demonstrated their support for Fauci as the crisis was unfolding. Along with participating in the Zoom call, the former couple donned matching black hoodies emblazoned with the wording "Fauci Gang" for an Instagram post that Bloom shared in May 2020.
"Double tap if you’re in the #drfauci gang," Bloom wrote in the caption.

The hoodies were created as part of a Jerry Media x PizzaSlime collaboration and priced at $69. According to Bustle, the first batch of hoodies quickly sold out after their release. A portion of the proceeds from each sale benefited the CDC Foundation's Coronavirus Emergency Response Fund.
Jennifer Garner
Jennifer Garner said she loved Fauci ahead of interviewing him. (Chris Haston/WBTV via Getty Images)
Jennifer Garner publicly praised Fauci before hosting the infectious disease expert for a lengthy Instagram Live in September 2020 in which they discussed parents' concerns during the pandemic.

Garner later shared the interview in an Instagram post, writing in the caption, "Conversation with Dr. Fauci Back-to-School/vaccine/sports/and more questions answered here. I love Dr. Fauci—and you will, too."
The actress and Fauci's conversation spanned a wide range of topics, including schools reopening, youth sports, vaccines, vitamins, flu shots and when Americans could safely return to movie theaters.
During the interview, Garner expressed her gratitude to Fauci, telling him, "I just wanted to start by just saying thank you for never lying to us. Thank you for always giving it to us straight."
"I know that you have saved, I mean, countless lives," she added.
TOM HANKS JOKES ABOUT THE NAME HE WOULD GIVE CORONAVIRUS VACCINE
Leonardo DiCaprio
Leonardo DiCaprio paid tribute to Fauci at a virtual gala. (Jason Armond)

Leonardo DiCaprio honored Fauci during the National Italian American Foundation's 2020 virtual gala, where the infectious disease expert received the Leonardo da Vinci Award for Leadership in Health and Science.

"While COVID is keeping most of us at home, people like Dr. Fauci go to work each morning with one goal: to see our nation through the most devastating pandemic in a century," DiCaprio said via the Washingtonian.
"I am delighted that NIAF is honoring his lifelong commitment to serving the public good, we are fortunate to have Dr Fauci's leadership and guidance in these difficult times," he added.

Other celebrities who shared tributes to Fauci at the gala included Al Pacino, Robert De Niro, Martin Scorsese, Francis Ford Coppola, Michael Douglas, Patti LuPone, Bono, Marisa Tomei, Alan Alda, Dionne Warwick and Angelica Huston.
Matthew McConaughey
Matthew McConaughey discussed myths and vaccines with Fauci during a 40-minute conversation in August 2020. (Getty Images)
Matthew McConaughey gave Fauci one of his biggest celebrity platforms during the pandemic when he interviewed the infectious disease expert on Instagram in August 2020.

During their 40-minute conversation, McConaughey and Fauci discussed COVID-19 myths and vaccines. The Oscar winner expressed his anger and disappointment over how he felt the virus had become "politicized."
"Like a lot of people, I've been more than disillusioned — actually quite full of rage — at how COVID has been politicized," McConaughey said.

The actor closed their conversation by embracing Fauci's call for Americans to "pull together" as the former Chief Medical Advisor to the President noted they had done in the aftermath of World War II and 9/11.
"This is equivalent to that, Matthew. We've got to pull together, absolutely," Fauci said.
"That's it," McConaughey said. "We can have our freedom and our party later. Right now, let's pull together."
Alyssa Milano
Alyssa Milano vocally defended Fauci during the pandemic. (Gerardo Mora/Getty Images)

Alyssa Milano was among Hollywood's most vocal defenders of Fauci during the pandemic. The actress frequently shared his interviews on social media, encouraged followers to trust the nation's top infectious disease expert and repeatedly criticized political attacks against him as debates over masks, shutdowns and vaccines intensified.

However, Milano, who is a longtime critic of President Donald Trump, publicly expressed frustration with Fauci as she shared her opinion that he hadn't been outspoken enough in challenging the administration's response to the pandemic.

"Dr. Fauci might be great and a national treasure, but please let us not forget that he just sat there as Trump made ridiculous uneducated public health claims," she wrote on X in July 2020. "He has also allowed the White House to silence him as things continued to spiral out of control."
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS
Mark Ruffalo
Mark Ruffalo praised Fauci for "speaking truth to power." (Lia Toby/Getty Images)
Mark Ruffalo repeatedly praised Fauci and amplified the infectious disease expert on social media. In an April 2020 post on X, Ruffalo wrote, "Thank you Dr. Fauci for speaking truth to power."

Throughout the pandemic, Ruffalo shared the doctor's public health guidance with his followers, including posting Fauci's interviews along with vaccine information and messages encouraging Americans to follow scientific recommendations.

As criticism of Fauci intensified in mid-2020, Ruffalo often defended the infectious disease expert on social media. He amplified stories defending Fauci and called attention to what he viewed as attacks on public health experts.

George Takei
George Takei consistently supported Fauci. (Tommaso Boddi/Getty Images for AMC)

George Takei was one of Fauci's most consistent celebrity supporters on social media. The "Star Trek" actor celebrated former President Joe Biden's decision to keep Fauci as chief medical adviser when he took office in January 2021.
In an X post he shared in December 2020, Takei shared a clip about Fauci continuing his role in Biden's administration, writing, "Wonderful news, indeed."
Throughout 2020 and beyond, Takei used his large social media following to defend Fauci, praise his work and criticize attacks on him.

title: Trace Adkins survived ex-wife's 'kill shot' after bullet passed through heart and lungs
summary: Trace Adkins revealed on Theo Von's podcast how ex-wife Julie Curtis shot him through the heart and both lungs in 1994 in what he called a "kill shot."
story: Grammy-winning country star Trace Adkins talks to Fox News Digital about his new single ‘American Made’ and why now is the perfect time for a song reminding Americans of American greatness. (Credit: Nicholas Ballasy for Fox News Digital)
Trace Adkins is going into detail about how he survived a "kill shot" from one of his ex-wives.

During a recent appearance on the "This Past Weekend with Theo Von" podcast, the 64-year-old country singer discussed his four marriages and how one of his exes "took it a little far" when asking him to leave, and shot him.
"She was mad. Wanted me to leave, and I wasn't going to leave, so that's how it went down," he said. "She put it under my left arm and the bullet came out under my right arm."
He went on to share that as she was holding the gun and preparing to fire it, he approached her with his hand out, asking her to give him the gun when she fired the shot.
Adkins discussed the circumstances surrounding one of his ex-wives shooting him during a recent podcast appearance. (Jason Kempin/Getty Images)
COUNTRY SINGER RAELYNN FILES FOR DIVORCE FROM ARMY VETERAN HUSBAND AFTER DECADE-LONG MARRIAGE

When asked what it felt like to be shot, Adkins explained that in his opinion, when the situation "is that serious, your body protects you," and "you just go into shock," adding that he doesn't remember feeling anything.

"I just remember getting up off the floor and then taking a few steps and then going back down and that's all I remember," he said. It went under this arm, came out this arm. So it went straight through. It went straight through my heart and both my lungs. It was a kill shot."

The "Ladies Love Country Boys" singer added: "The doctor said the only reason I survived was cause the bullet went through at point-blank velocity at muzzle velocity. So it didn't have time to mushroom. It was just muzzle velocity, so it just went straight through."
He went on to say that the pain from his injury came during the recovery process, saying that in order to repair his heart and lungs, "they just cut you and just crack you open."
Adkins said the only reason he survived was because he was shot at such close range. (Jason Kempin)
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR THE ENTERTAINMENT NEWSLETTER

When asked if he thought she was trying to end his life by shooting him, Adkins said he doesn't think so, adding, "I don't think she even had any idea what that gun was going to do." In the end, the singer decided not to press charges against his ex.

"I'd never seen her hold a gun. I'd never seen her shoot a gun," he said. "I knew she had one, but I'd never seen her use it. I had a bunch of guns, still have a bunch of guns, and I shoot them pretty often, but I'd never seen her do that. And I just I don't think she knew what was about to happen when she pulled that trigger. She thought it was a toy."

The incident took place in 1994, when he separated from his second wife, Julie Curtis, with the couple getting divorced later that year. Prior to Curtis, the singer was married to Barbara Lewis, and later went on to marry Rhonda Forlaw, who he separated from in 2014.
He is now married to Canadian actress Victoria Pratt, who he married in October 2019 in a ceremony officiated by singer Blake Shelton.

"She is so proud to be an American," he said. "My family's been here for over eight generations on both sides. I'm proud to be an American too, and you know, I think we're equally as proud so there you go."

title: Kelsey Grammer suspects he 'may have' lost Hollywood roles due to conservative views
summary: Kelsey Grammer suspects being a conservative in Hollywood for 40 years may have kept him off casting lists and out of awards conversations entirely.
story: Kelsey Grammer told Fox News Digital that the key to success in America is hard work and hurting as few people in the process.
Kelsey Grammer suggested his decades-long embrace of conservative politics may have come at a professional cost.
The "Frasier" star said he couldn't say for certain whether his politics had cost him work, but he believed his conservative views may have kept him off Hollywood's radar altogether.

"I have no idea," he said when asked whether he'd ever lost a role because of his political views during an appearance on "The Katie Miller Podcast." "I suspect I may have, but I suspect I may be, you know, in that category where they just don't even think about me, so it’s okay."
"'Oh, we wouldn't work with him, he's a conservative,'" he mused. "I hope that's not the case because I'm actually pretty good at what I do."
DWAYNE 'THE ROCK' JOHNSON REJECTS HOLLYWOOD’S POLITICAL OBSESSION, BLASTS CELEBRITY ATTACK CULTURE

Kelsey Grammer said he suspects his longtime conservative political views may have cost him opportunities in Hollywood, while arguing politics shouldn't influence casting or awards decisions. (Randy Shropshire/Getty Images for Paramount+)

Grammer said the same political dynamics extended beyond casting decisions and into Hollywood's biggest honors. The 71-year-old actor argued political leanings had possibly become part of the equation when performances alone should decide who gets recognized.

"You know, there's always been sort of a popularity contest with awards anyway," Grammer explained. "And you surprise them a little bit, you do something good once in a while that might get attention. But there's so many overlays of what people will vote for and not vote for."

"I mean, politically, I'm kind of, you know, on the fringe of Hollywood. It's okay, I don’t mind, because I've been a, I'm a conservative. I've been a conservative in Hollywood for 40 years. I declared early. So, it’s been okay. They're kind of used to it with me," he added. "But there are other concerns that actually probably shouldn't enter into it. It shouldn't be politics. It should be performance, you know."
Kelsey Grammer's portrayal of psychiatrist Dr. Frasier Crane on "Cheers" paved the way for the Emmy-winning sitcom "Frasier," cementing his TV legacy. (NBCUniversal via Getty Images)
Grammer said he had privately found support from others in the entertainment industry who shared his political views but had chosen not to express them publicly.
"There's several of us in the closet," he admitted. "There's never those who aren't in the closet. Some of us who left the acting profession entirely."
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR THE ENTERTAINMENT NEWSLETTER
Kelsey Grammer won multiple Emmy Awards for his portrayal of Dr. Frasier Crane, turning the psychiatrist into one of television's most beloved sitcom characters. (Bob Riha, Jr./Getty Images)
Grammer also weighed in on the state of television comedy, arguing modern sitcoms had lost the qualities that once made them resonate with audiences.

"...as a format, it's struggling again for the right writers and for trust in the human experience. They don't trust their audience anymore," the actor explained on the podcast. "And the key, the key to ‘Frasier's' success, was that it trusted the audience."

"It thought it was smart enough, and we thought they were intelligent enough to enjoy discovering that we had a family and lives and things we cared about, as well as being funny," Grammer added. "And they've lost that again."
When asked whether Hollywood writers had become too disconnected from audiences by embracing political correctness and an insular industry mindset, Grammer said one factor stood out.

Kelsey Grammer suggested Hollywood comedy has lost touch with audiences, saying political correctness has "probably" hurt the creative process and changed what writers think is funny. (Mathew Tsang/Getty Images)
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

"The idea of being too politically correct is probably killing the process, I think," the "Cheers" star said. "It's not necessarily destroyed funny for everyone. It's just, they've eliminated funny based upon human behavior. They've made it just too on point on people that don't actually behave that way."

"But, so, I think it may have maybe made a big wrong turn in terms of what people think is funny. It's mostly slapstick, and you have to earn slapstick to make it believable," Grammer noted. "If it's not believable, it's just a terrible joke. And I think that's where they've gone mostly."

Kelsey Grammer's portrayal of Dr. Frasier Crane helped make "Frasier" one of the most acclaimed sitcoms in TV history, with the series earning dozens of Emmy Awards during its run. (NBCUniversal via Getty Images)

Grammer has become one of TV's most recognizable stars thanks to his decades-long career in drama and comedy. He landed his big break in 1984 with "Cheers." Playing the supporting role of psychiatrist Dr. Frasier Crane eventually led to the long-running spin-off "Frasier," which earned him multiple Emmy Awards and cemented his place in TV history.

title: '80s icon Kristy McNichol makes rare appearance 25 years after leaving Hollywood
summary: Kristy McNichol, who retired from Hollywood in 2001 after starring in "Family" and "Empty Nest," was spotted in a rare new photo with Carnie Wilson.
story: Carnie Wilson told Fox News Digital that some days are more challenging than others, but connection with others and staying positive makes her feel better.
Famous '80s icon Kristy McNichol made a rare appearance this week in a new photo with Carnie Wilson — 25 years after leaving Hollywood.
On July 20, the 58-year-old Wilson Philips singer shared a selfie on Facebook in which she was seen with the 63-year-old retired actress and gushed over her encounter with one of her childhood idols.
"Totally fangirling!!!" Wilson wrote in the caption. "Kris (Kristy McNichol) was a part of my youth. I adored her in her movies... Especially Little Darlings and The End."

'80s star Kristy McNichol made a rare appearance in a selfie with Carnie Wilson decades after leaving Hollywood. (Carnie Wilson Facebook; ABC Photo Archives/Disney General Entertainment Content via Getty Images)

Wilson went on to say that she told McNichol "how meaningful" her movies were to her and her close friend Tiffany Miller. The five-time Grammy Award nominee said she also shared that she and Miller were "JUST TALKING" about McNichol and "how special she is."
HEATHER LOCKLEAR SAYS SHE LIVES 'FAR AWAY' FROM HOLLYWOOD AND STAYS OUT OF THE SOCIAL SCENE
"What a gracious sweetie," Wilson added with a string of red heart emojis. "She sure is loved."

In the photo, McNichol was seen wearing a navy blue and red fleece jacket over a white T-shirt along with gold earrings. Wilson was clad in a black top with a brightly colored leaf pattern and a black beanie. The pair beamed as they stood close together and posed for the camera.
MELISSA GILBERT, MICHAEL LANDON AND MORE: WHERE THE ORIGINAL 'LITTLE HOUSE ON THE PRAIRIE' CAST IS NOW
McNichol launched her career as a child actor, starring in commercials and making guest appearances in hit sitcoms including "Starsky & Hutch," "CHiPs" and "The Love Boat."
The actress landed her first role as a series regular when she starred as Patricia Apple in the CBS drama series "Apple's Way" for two seasons from 1974 to 1975.
SALLY FIELD SAYS BURT REYNOLDS WAS ‘WONDERFUL’ BUT ‘FRIGHTENING,’ CLAIMS HE TRIED TO CONTROL HER CAREER

McNichol made her breakthrough in 1976 at age 14, when she was tapped to play Letitia "Buddy" Lawrence in the ABC drama series "Family." The role earned her two Primetime Emmy Awards and launched her as one of television's biggest teen stars.
BO DEREK REVEALS WHY SHE FELT LIKE AN 'IMPOSTOR' AND WALKED AWAY FROM HOLLYWOOD DESPITE BLOCKBUSTER FAME
McNichol made her breakthrough when she starred in the hit drama series "Family." (ABC Photo Archives/Disney General Entertainment Content via Getty Images)

In 1977, McNichol began acting in movies and starred in the 1978 black comedy "The End" with Burt Reynolds and Sally Field. She won critical acclaim when she starred as Angel Bright in the hit 1980 teen comedy-drama "Little Darlings" alongside Tatum O'Neal, Matt Dillon and Armand Assante.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR THE ENTERTAINMENT NEWSLETTER

McNichol went on to star in the hit movies "The Night the Lights Went Out in Georgia" (1980) and "Only When I Laugh" (1981), the latter of which earned her a Golden Globe nomination for best supporting actress.
She also played leading roles in "The Pirate Movie" (1982), "Dream Lover" (1986) and "You Can't Hurry Love" (1988).
Matt Dillon starred with McNichol in the film "Little Darlings." (Michael Ochs Archives/Getty Images)

In 1986, she returned to TV full-time with a starring role on the sitcom "Empty Nest," which was a spin-off of the iconic sitcom "The Golden Girls." McNichol made her last on-screen appearance in the 1995 season finale of "Empty Nest" after stepping away from the show in 1992.
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS
In 2001, McNichol announced that she was retiring from acting. "A lot of people have wondered what I've been up to," she said in a statement. "I retired from my career after 24 years."

"My feeling was that it was time to play my biggest part – myself!" McNichol continued. "I must say that it has been the best thing that ever happened to me. So many fans are disappointed that I'm not currently acting; however, some may not realize that the process I'm in at this time is necessary and vital for my personal happiness and well-being."
McNichol (pictured in 2014) has largely stayed out of the spotlight since retiring. (Bobby Bank/WireImage)

Since leaving the entertainment industry, McNichol has largely stayed out of the public eye. During a rare interview with People magazine in 2014, McNichol explained that she left Hollywood to "see what else was out there."
"I was on the big stage between ages 8 and 30," McNichol said. "I left show business for a variety of reasons, but a big one was my interest in learning what else there is in life."

"This phase of my life is so good," she shared. "My home life is happy and serene. I love singing. I also enjoy traveling and seeing the world. One of my favorite stops is Hawaii. I like everything about it and may eventually move there part-time."

While speaking with the outlet, McNichol did not rule out eventually making an acting comeback.
"Never say never," she said.

title: Jelly Roll and Bunnie Xo take different paths after divorce as he climbs mountains, she buys $500K Rolls-Royce
summary: Bunnie Xo's new Rolls Royce, Nashville mansion and younger new boyfriend contrast sharply with Jelly Roll's fitness journey and new song release.
story: Jelly Roll tells Fox News Digital what it means to him to celebrate the 60th Academy of Country Music Awards.
Jelly Roll and Bunnie Xo may have ended their marriage together, but they're embracing dramatically different next acts.
As Bunnie Xo stepped into a world of luxury and fresh romance rumors, the country star doubled down on fitness, fresh music and major career wins.

Jelly Roll filed for divorce from Bunnie Xo on May 18, but the "Son of a Sinner" singer listed the date of separation as May 9. The two first met in 2015 after the former sex worker met the rising star at a concert in Las Vegas and eloped a year later.
Bunnie Xo and Jelly Roll were married nearly 10 years before their divorce was finalized in July.
JELLY ROLL FILES FOR DIVORCE FROM WIFE BUNNIE XO AFTER ALMOST A DECADE OF MARRIAGE

Jelly Roll and Bunnie Xo have embraced dramatically different post-divorce chapters, with the country star focusing on his health while the podcast host has showcased a lavish new lifestyle. (Taylor Hill/Getty Images)

If there were any questions about what Bunnie Xo's next chapter would look like, she answered them with a string of eye-catching reveals that painted a picture of luxury, independence and a fresh start.
Post-divorce, Bunnie Xo splurged on a brand new Rolls-Royce. "Sometimes a girl needs to spoil herself," she captioned a video showcasing her new ride, which is estimated to cost roughly $500,000.

Bunnie Xo also gave her social media followers a tour of her new Nashville-area home, which included hidden stairways, multiple massive closets, opulent floral rooms, an outdoor shower and an infinity pool.
BUNNIE XO SAYS SHE FUNDED JELLY ROLL'S EARLY CAREER BY 'TURNING TRICKS' WHILE REFLECTING ON DIVORCE

After nearly 10 years of marriage, Jelly Roll has documented his fitness journey as Bunnie Xo has shared glimpses of luxury purchases, including a reported $500,000 Rolls-Royce and a new Nashville-area home. (Christopher Polk/Penske Media via Getty Images)

As Bunnie Xo's post-divorce life played out on social media, Jelly Roll's next chapter centered on self-improvement.

"Just a few years ago, I finally threw my Hands Up and started changing my life," he wrote in the caption. "Today I'm throwing my hands up on top of a MOUNTAIN we decided to hike on a whim that would have been literally impossible for me to get up not long ago."
"God is GREAT y'all, God is so great."

Jelly Roll has celebrated new health milestones and music releases following his divorce from Bunnie Xo, while the podcast host has turned heads with her extravagant post-split lifestyle. (Getty Images)
JELLY ROLL ADMITS ONE MISTAKE SENT HIM ON A FOOD BINGE AMID BUNNIE XO DIVORCE
The country star has continued to chronicle nearly every step of his health journey, celebrating both major milestones and the everyday habits that have fueled his transformation.
Jelly Roll recently shared a recipe for a protein shake that he actually enjoys as the 41-year-old singer gave a weight loss update on his Instagram.
"Swole Roll otw," he captioned the post.
Despite charting separate paths, Jelly Roll and Bunnie Xo have remained united on one point: shutting down rumors about what led to their divorce.
Bunnie Xo and Jelly Roll (born Jason DeFord) have fiercely defended their private relationship after news of their split broke the internet with accusations of cheating.
Terms of their settlement remain confidential. However, People reported the former couple will split their assets, including homes, cars, an aircraft and any intellectual property.

Jelly Roll and Bunnie Xo finalized their divorce in July, but the former couple has continued making headlines as they navigate strikingly different paths after their split. (Kevin Mazur / Getty Images for The Recording Academy)

Despite untangling their finances and officially ending their marriage, Jelly Roll and Bunnie Xo made it clear they weren't severing every tie.
"We're literally settling our divorce in like... We've done it in like, what? Three weeks? Two weeks?" Bunnie Xo said in a since-deleted episode of her podcast. "We're still having a baby together."

Although the terms of their divorce remain confidential, Jelly Roll and Bunnie Xo said they're moving forward with plans to have a child together. (Gilbert Flores/Penske Media via Getty Images)

title: Monica Lewinsky's Lindsey Graham tribute draws criticism and praise for placing people over party: expert
summary: Experts say Monica Lewinsky's tribute to Lindsey Graham after his death reflects her philosophy of people over party despite political disagreements.
story: Activist Monica Lewinsky told Fox News Digital that her personal definition of power has evolved over the years.

Monica Lewinsky's tribute to Lindsey Graham following his death sparked interest across the aisles, not only for her respectful candor, but also served as a reminder of the late senator's impact on history.
Lewinsky, 53, paid her respects to the late South Carolina senator shortly after his death earlier this month and gave followers insight on their decades-long connection.
Her non-partisan testimonial drew criticism online, but experts believed that her tribute was an authentic gesture which reflected her personal philosophy of people over party.
MONICA LEWINSKY RECALLS 'VERY DARK MOMENTS' AFTER SCANDAL, SURVIVING JUDGMENT BY 'BILLIONS OF STRANGERS'
Monica Lewinsky's tribute to late Senator Lindsey Graham drew criticism and praise. (Jamie McCarthy/WireImage/Getty Images)
Graham, who died July 11 after what his office described was a "brief and sudden illness," was one of the Republican Party's most influential voices with more than three decades of service.
His death prompted thousands of tributes, including one poignant message from the former White House intern.
MONICA LEWINSKY SAYS BILL CLINTON ‘ESCAPED A LOT MORE THAN I DID’ AFTER WHITE HOUSE SCANDAL

"I've disagreed with many (many) of Lindsey Graham’s choices and beliefs, but he was also — as one of the house managers on the '98 impeachment — the one who worked tirelessly to prove there was a smear campaign against me from inside the WH," Lewinsky posted on X shortly after his death.
When X users took umbrage with the homage, Lewinsky was quick to remind followers that her experience was "healing" after years of trauma from the Clinton scandal.
"Come on. He did not do it for you. The man was evil," one user wrote.
Lewinsky fired back, "I know he didn’t do it for me. i didn’t whitewash his history. but those actions were healing for me (and my family)… thanks for sharing your opinion."
SEN. LINDSEY GRAHAM DEAD AT 71 AFTER 'BRIEF AND SUDDEN' ILLNESS, OFFICE SAYS
Monica Lewinsky was 21 when she began an unpaid internship at the White House under the Clinton administration. (Getty Images)
Adrienne Uthe, founder of Kronus Communications, exclusively told Fox News Digital that Lewinsky's tribute "fits her clearly identified personal philosophy to a tee."

"She's not suddenly a Lindsey Graham fan — she's just honest enough to say he did one thing that mattered to her, and she's not going to let political disagreement erase that," Uthe said. "It works in her favor, and it's the kind of nuance that actually means something."
Uthe noted that Lewinsky's post was "nonchalant, direct, and completely unpolished in the best way."

"There's no performance to it — it reads like: 'Hey, he wasn't perfect, I disagreed with most of what he did, but he did this one thing for me and I appreciated it.' That's it. It's classy, and it's a stand-up thing to highlight in someone's death."
"She's not suddenly a Lindsey Graham fan — she's just honest enough to say he did one thing that mattered to her, and she's not going to let political disagreement erase that."

Lewinsky was 21 years old when she began an unpaid internship at the White House in July 1995. She turned 22 that summer, and her sexual relationship with former President Bill Clinton, who was 49 at the time, began in November 1995.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR THE ENTERTAINMENT NEWSLETTER

It was only after she confided in a Pentagon co-worker, Linda Tripp – who secretly recorded their conversations, which were then used in Paula Jones' sexual harassment lawsuit against Clinton – when the affair became public fodder.
Lindsey Graham was one of 13 house members who served in Clinton's impeachment trial. (David Hume Kennerly)
Graham argued during the hearings that former President Bill Clinton abused his powers. (Karin Cooper)

During a January 1998 White House news conference, Clinton famously denied the affair, and stated, "I did not have sexual relations with that woman, Miss Lewinsky," and Lewinsky subsequently went into hiding due to public humiliation.

Graham was one of the 13 House members appointed to Clinton's impeachment trial, where he not only blasted the former president for lying under oath, but also argued to restore "honor and integrity to the office."

"You don’t even have to be convicted of a crime to lose your job in this constitutional republic if this body determines that your conduct as a public official is clearly out of bounds in your role," he said on the floor in January 1999.
"Impeachment is not about punishment. Impeachment is about cleansing the office. Impeachment is about restoring honor and integrity to the office."
"Impeachment is not about punishment. Impeachment is about cleansing the office. Impeachment is about restoring honor and integrity to the office."
The impeachment trial against the 42nd president began in January 1999 and ended Feb. 12. While Clinton was impeached by the house, he was acquitted of perjury and obstruction of justice charges.
Monica Lewinsky became a household name and was hounded in public following the affair. (Jeffrey Markowitz)

Holly Baird, crisis management expert and founder of Media Source PR, told Fox News Digital that Lewinsky's tribute made it clear that her appreciation for the late senator was limited to specific circumstances and "should not be interpreted as agreement with his broader political positions."
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

"Lewinsky's advocacy has centered on fairness, empathy, and the lasting impact of public treatment," Baird said. "Acknowledging someone she disagreed with politically for treating her fairly is consistent with those broader themes and reflects the principles she has consistently emphasized throughout her public life."
She added, "The statement reflects the idea that personal gratitude and political disagreement can coexist."

"Acknowledging someone she disagreed with politically for treating her fairly is consistent with those broader themes and reflects the principles she has consistently emphasized throughout her public life."

Former White House spokesperson Alexandra LaManna, noted how Lewinsky has dedicated her life to "turning one of the most public personal humiliations in modern history into something that has helped countless other people feel seen."
Monica Lewinsky's mother, Marcia Lewis, testified before a grand jury about the presidential affair and alleged cover-up. (Larry Morris/The Washington Post)
Monica Lewinsky was honored earlier this year as the 2026 Woman of the 21st Century by the Women's Guild Cedars-Sinai. (ABImages)
"By speaking openly about her own experience, she has helped change the way we think about public shaming, power imbalances, and being defined by the worst moment of your life," LaManna said.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"So when she thanks Lindsey Graham for standing up for her at a time when almost no one else did, it doesn't read as politics – it reads as someone recognizing decency where she found it, even in a complicated story."
"By speaking openly about her own experience, she has helped change the way we think about public shaming, power imbalances, and being defined by the worst moment of your life."

Shortly after Graham's death, his sister, Sen. Darline Graham, R-S.C., was appointed to temporarily fill her brother's seat. She later announced on Fox News that she would enter next month’s special primary election to run for a full term in the Senate.

title: White House fires back after John Mellencamp mocks Trump's Gulf of America during concert
summary: John Mellencamp paused his "Pink Houses" performance to mock Trump's Gulf of America executive order, prompting a sharp White House response.
story: Fox News Flash top entertainment and celebrity headlines are here.

Mellencamp paused his Saturday night show Holmdel, N.J. to mock Trump's executive order to rename the "Gulf of Mexico" to "Gulf of America."
On Monday, Davis Ingle, WH Spokesman, shared a statement with Fox News Digital. "Nobody in their right mind cares what out-of-touch, woke Hollywood celebrities have to say," Ingle said.
John Mellencamp blasted President Donald Trump's Gulf of America name change during a recent show. (Phillip Faraone/Getty Images for The Recording Academy)

WHITE HOUSE FIRES BACK AFTER ROBERT DE NIRO, BRUCE SPRINGSTEEN TAKE TRUMP SWIPES AMID COLBERT'S FAREWELL WEEK

"Nobody in their right mind cares what out-of-touch, woke Hollywood celebrities have to say."
While Mellencamp's band kept playing, the musician said sarcastically, "The Gulf of Mexico? Is that right? It’s not the Gulf of America? What a stupid f–----g idea."

President Donald Trump held a "Gulf of America" hat on the South Lawn of the White House in April 2025. (Yuri Gripas/Abaca/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

story: Brooks Nader tells Fox News Digital about growing up with conservative parents who banned two-piece bikinis and reveals why her "Baywatch" swimsuit gets the family seal of approval at FOX Upfront 2026 red carpet.

BROOKS NADER NARROWLY AVOIDS WARDROBE MALFUNCTION MINUTES BEFORE 'BAYWATCH' REBOOT RED CARPET
Brooks Nader suffered an accidental wardrobe malfunction after enjoying a beach day at the iconic Club 55 in Saint-Tropez. (Backgrid)

Brooks Nader is enjoying time in Saint-Tropez, France with friends. (Aissaoui Nacer/ Splash by Shutterstock)

BROOKS NADER WOWS IN ICONIC RED ONE-PIECE BATHING SUIT AS 'BAYWATCH' REBOOT FILMS BEACH SCENES

title: Kelly Ripa's painful surgery leaves her unable to speak
summary: Mark Consuelos revealed Kelly Ripa's gum graft surgery left her unable to talk, sharing details of her painful recovery with guest Nick Jonas.
story: Fox News Flash top entertainment and celebrity headlines are here.
Kelly Ripa's painful dental surgery sidelined the daytime TV staple, forcing the famously chatty host into an unusual recovery that left husband Mark Consuelos revealing she couldn't even speak.
During Monday's show, Consuelos revealed Ripa had undergone gum graft surgery.
"Kelly sends her love," the "Live with Kelly and Mark" co-host told guest Nick Jonas. "Kelly had a little bit – well, it’s not a little – she had a gum graft surgery."
Gum graft surgery typically helps correct thinning or receding gums, according to Cleveland Clinic. Consuelos admitted Ripa had been recommended to have the surgery years ago.
CLAY AIKEN SAYS KELLY RIPA FEUD SPARKED THE 'MOST CATASTROPHIC' WEEK OF HIS LIFE
Kelly Ripa is recovering from a painful gum graft surgery that forced the daytime TV host to stop talking, according to husband Mark Consuelos. (Dia Dipasupil/WireImage)
"Her dentist said five years ago, ‘You can do it in about five years,’" Consuelos recalled. "And she joked, ‘I didn’t think I’d still be on the air in five years!’"
Consuelos revealed her lengthy recovery process includes not talking.
"Wow. That’s got to be the hardest thing she’s ever done," Jonas joked.
Describing Ripa as "such a great conversationalist," Consuelos hinted he might be having trouble getting the talk show host to follow doctor's orders.
"I’m trying to keep her to follow the rules, follow the directions," he said.
KELLY RIPA SAYS 'DESPERATE TIMES' LED HER TO GET COSMETIC PROCEDURE DONE ON HER BACKSIDE

Mark Consuelos revealed Kelly Ripa's unusually painful dental surgery has sidelined the "Live with Kelly and Mark" co-host, saying the recovery has been one of her toughest yet. (Jeff Kravitz/FilmMagic)
As Ripa recovered at home, Consuelos said the toughest part wasn't the pain – it was convincing the famously curious TV host to stop checking on her healing gums and let the procedure do its work.

"Last night she was like, ‘Can you look?’ I’m like, ‘I’m not pulling your lip down,’" Consuelos said. Ripa instead got into position so Consuelos could check without touching her lip. "So I’m down there like, ‘It looks great!’"

Despite famously skipping novocaine at the dentist, Kelly Ripa admitted defeat after a painful gum graft surgery left her recovering at home and away from "Live with Kelly and Mark." (Lorenzo Bevilaqua/Disney via Getty Images)
The longtime actor said the surgery was especially alarming because Ripa rarely complains about pain, making this recovery stand out from any previous trip to the dentist.
"Yeah, it’s painful," he told Jonas. "But she famously doesn’t feel pain. When she goes into the dentist, she doesn’t use the novocaine. But this one hurts, so I know it’s bad."
Ripa's notoriously high pain tolerance led Jonas to marvel at just how much women can endure. He revealed his own wife, Danielle Jonas, has a similar ability to brush off pain.

Nick Jonas joked that Kelly Ripa's doctor-ordered silence "has got to be the hardest thing she's ever done" after Mark Consuelos revealed the TV host underwent gum graft surgery. (Kevin Mazur/Getty Images for Live Nation)

"Well, they do have kids. They deliver kids," Consuelos added. "We’re not built for that."
Ripa is not expected to return to "Live" for the next week, a representative for the show confirmed to People.

title: 'You're So Vain' singer Carly Simon says Parkinson's and cancer diagnoses kept her from public eye
summary: "You're So Vain" singer Carly Simon reveals her Parkinson's disease diagnosis and basal cell carcinoma surgery, explaining why she withdrew from the public spotlight.
story: The co-founder of The Michael J. Fox Foundation called it "powerful" to see two Parkinson's patients interacting with one another.
Carly Simon has Parkinson's disease and underwent surgery for basal cell carcinoma, a form of skin cancer.
The "You're So Vain" singer told People magazine in a statement published July 27 why she had recently stayed out of the spotlight.

"It has taken me some time to understand the diagnosis, to adjust to it, and to decide how much I wanted to say about it publicly," the 83-year-old told the outlet. "Parkinson's is different for everyone, and it can be unpredictable. Some days I'm so tired I can't get the day moving at all. On others, it gives me a little more room to move, think, work and feel like myself."
MICHAEL J. FOX SAYS GOING PUBLIC WITH PARKINSON'S WAS 'HELL' ON WIFE TRACY POLLAN

On July 27, 2026, Carly Simon told People magazine in a statement that she has Parkinson’s disease and underwent surgery for basal cell carcinoma, a form of skin cancer. "I have not stopped living, and I have not stopped working," she told the outlet. (Jack Mitchell/Getty Images)

"The problems began with arthritis in both knees and one hip," the star shared. "I eventually had all three joints replaced, out with the old and in with delicate bouquets of metal and plastic. After three replacement surgeries, I assumed my difficulty walking was simply an unfortunate and rather ironic part of the recovery process."

According to Simon, her mobility continued to worsen. She struggled to stand from "low chairs and deep couches" without someone offering help. "Overstuffed furniture became my enemy," she recalled. There were periods when she couldn't walk "without considerable help."
Simon knew something was wrong.
WATCH: DEBORAH W. BROOKS COMMENDS MICHAEL J. FOX FOR HIS 'COURAGE' TO LIVE OPENLY WITH PARKINSON'S
It wasn't until she underwent an extensive evaluation at the Mayo Clinic that Simon was diagnosed with Parkinson's disease. She soon began treatment to help manage stiffness and other symptoms.
"Parkinson's is usually associated with movement, tremors and balance, but it can affect much more than the body," Simon explained.

"It can bring anxiety, depression, exhaustion and apathy. The apathy is particularly strange. You can find yourself lying there like a starfish drying in the sun, arms pointing in all directions, while nothing inside is telling you to get up, read, watch, write, sing, call someone or do much of anything at all. ... It is not simply sadness or laziness. It is as though the part of the brain that sends out invitations to participate in life has temporarily misplaced the guest list."

Carly Simon performs during the 2017 Tribeca Film Festival Opening Gala premiere of "Clive Davis: The Soundtrack of Our Lives" at Radio City Music Hall on April 19, 2017, in New York City. (Clint Spaulding/WWD/Penske Media via Getty Images)

During this period, Simon was treated for basal cell carcinoma on her face. While surgeons removed the skin cancer, the procedure left her self-conscious about her appearance and reluctant to be seen in public.

"I have always been more critical of my appearance than anyone else could possibly imagine (check out the irony of having written 'You're So Vain'), and this gave my inner critic quite a lot of new material," Simon wrote.

"Between my mobility issues, the Parkinson's diagnosis, the surgery and the emotional effects of it all, withdrawing from public view was the most palatable reaction," Simon said. "If a person is allowed to hibernate during both winter and summer, then I have become an all-season bear."
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR THE ENTERTAINMENT NEWSLETTER
Recording artist Carly Simon stands for a portrait in New York City on June 18, 2008. She lives on Martha's Vineyard. (Daniel Acker/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

Despite her personal struggles, Simon stressed that she has "not stopped living, and I have not stopped working." She quietly worked on a new album, "Comes in Waves," noting that music "has rescued me more times than I can count."
"Working on the music gave shape to days that did not always have much shape," Simon said. "... It reminded me that illness can change your life without becoming the whole of your life."

"I do not consider Parkinson's a gift or a blessing," she said. "It is neither. It is difficult, frustrating and sometimes frightening. I am still learning how to live with it and now how to accept it without feeling that I have surrendered something essential. I am still writing, singing, imagining, laughing, worrying, remembering and occasionally getting trapped in an overstuffed chair."
Carly Simon and Tony Shanahan pose backstage at the 31st Annual Tibet House US Benefit Concert and Gala at Carnegie Hall on March 3, 2018, in New York City. (Getty Images for Tibet House)

"I am deeply grateful to my children, my family, my friends, my caregivers and the medical professionals who have helped me through this," Simon said. "Their love and patience have carried me through days when my own reserves were not enough. I wanted to share this now because so many people have reached out with genuine concern. I am touched by that concern, even when I have not known how to respond."
"These days I move more slowly, I lean on others more than I once did, and I have learned to accept that every day will look a little different. But I am still very much here."
People reported that "Comes in Waves" is Simon's first full-length album since 2008.

Good friends Carly Simon and Jackie Onassis pose for a picture at Bunch of Grapes Bookstore on Martha's Vineyard, Massachusetts, on Sept. 2, 1989. (Stephen Rose/Getty Images)

Simon, who lives on Martha's Vineyard, made one of her last public appearances in 2019 when she visited SiriusXM Studios in New York City to promote her memoir, "Touched by the Sun: My Friendship with Jackie," which chronicles her once-close bond with former first lady Jacqueline Kennedy Onassis.
People reported that Simon's last public performance was in March 2018 at the 31st Annual Tibet House U.S. Benefit Concert & Gala at Carnegie Hall.

Musician Carly Simon (center) and sisters Lucy Simon and Joanna Simon attend The National Academy of Popular Music's 25th Annual Songwriters Hall of Fame Induction Ceremony on June 1, 1994, at Sheraton New York Hotel and Towers in New York City. (Ron Galella, Ltd./Ron Galella Collection via Getty Images)

Although Simon was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in November 2022, she did not attend the ceremony in Los Angeles. The event came weeks after her sisters, Joanna and Lucy Simon, died of cancer one day apart. People noted that Simon survived breast cancer after being diagnosed in 1997.

Olivia Rodrigo performs under a photo of Carly Simon during the 37th Annual Rock and Roll Hall of Fame Induction Ceremony at the Microsoft Theatre on Nov. 5, 2022, in Los Angeles. (AFP via Getty Images)

According to the Mayo Clinic, Parkinson's disease is a nervous system disorder that affects movement. Symptoms can include tremors, balance problems, stiffness, slowed movement and slurred speech. Although there is no cure for Parkinson's disease, medications and, in some cases, surgery can help manage symptoms.

Michael J. Fox, who was diagnosed with Parkinson's disease in 1991, was one of the first high-profile figures to raise public awareness of the disease. The "Back to the Future" star later founded the Michael J. Fox Foundation for Parkinson's Research.

Simon rose to fame with her 1971 self-titled debut album. The Grammy winner is best known for the 1972 hit "You're So Vain" and the James Bond theme "Nobody Does It Better," recorded for the 1977 film "The Spy Who Loved Me," starring Roger Moore as 007.
