title: Berlin Pride attack suspect killed in police confrontation: AP
summary: German authorities say Abdul Ballout, linked to Berlin's Islamist scene, was killed in a nearby suburb after the deadly attack near the Pride festival.
story: Fox News' Chanley Painter reports Berlin police are conducting a manhunt for 21-year-old Abdul B, identified as the suspect in a deadly van attack at a German Pride Festival. One person was killed and 16 others were injured after the van crashed into a crowd near the parade route. Authorities are investigating reports of additional stab wounds and suspect terrorism, noting the individual's ties to Islamic groups.

A suspect in the attack at Berlin's Pride festival that left one person dead and at least 29 others injured was killed during a confrontation with police in a nearby suburb, The Associated Press reported, citing authorities.

German authorities on Sunday launched an intensive manhunt for Abdul Ballout, a German citizen with Lebanese roots. Ballout was killed following a nearly 24-hour search. Prosecutors said he had previously sought to join the militant Islamic State group.
"Everything we see here points to us dealing with an Islamic terror attack," German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt said.
AT LEAST 1 DEAD, SEVERAL INJURED AFTER VAN RAMS INTO CROWD AT PRIDE FESTIVAL; SUSPECT 'KNOWN TO POLICE'
Abdul Ballout, a German citizen with Lebanese roots, was killed in a police confrontation after being sought in connection with the attack, authorities said. (Berlin Police)
The minister said the suspect had previously come to the attention of authorities for multiple crimes, as well as his "radicalization and belonging to the Islamist scene."

Dobrindt said Ballout was born in Germany and that his mother became a naturalized German citizen in 2002, three years before he was born. He said the suspect previously received a suspended prison sentence of one year and 10 months but did not disclose what he had been convicted of.
Police officers stand near a vehicle crashed into a tree after driving into a crowd near Berlin's annual Pride event, in Germany, Sunday, July 26, 2026. (AP Photo/Markus Schreiber)

Police said a white van drove into a crowd in Berlin's Tiergarten park around 10 p.m. on Saturday before crashing into a tree. Authorities say the suspect then attacked several people with a machete before fleeing.
WITNESSES RECOUNT 'SCARY' NYC STABBING AFTER SUSPECT ALLEGEDLY YELLED 'ALLAHU AKBAR' DURING ATTACKS
A woman was killed, while three people suffered life-threatening injuries and eight others were seriously hurt, according to Berlin's fire service. Dobrindt said at least 29 people were injured.
Emergency personnel and police gather in Berlin, early Sunday, July 26, 2026, following the cancellation of Christopher Street Day festivities. (AP Photo/Ebrahim Noroozi)

The attack happened a few hundred yards from Berlin's annual Christopher Street Day Pride celebration — one of Europe's largest LGBTQ+ events — but not on the parade route or at the festival's closing event near the Brandenburg Gate. Investigators said the victims appeared to include both Pride attendees and other people who were in the park.
Organizers stopped the celebration shortly after the attack, cutting off a live performance and urging people to leave the area.
People stand on 17 June Street following the cancellation of Christopher Street Day in Berlin on Saturday, July 25, 2026. (Fabian Sommer/DPA via AP)
SYNAGOGUE IN LONDON TARGETED IN ATTEMPTED 'ANTISEMITIC HATE CRIME,' UK POLICE SAY
Police spokesman Florian Nath earlier said the suspect was known to investigators because of his alleged ties to Islamic groups in Berlin.

"The suspect is known to police. He is known to us as a member of Islamic circles here in Berlin, and our search for this person is proceeding at full speed," Nath said, according to The Associated Press. "We still have no information whatsoever regarding his specific motives, the exact sequence of events, or his role in the crime itself."
Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt speaks to the media near the scene where a car rammed into a crowd at the Pride March in Berlin, Germany, Sunday, July 26, 2026. (AP Photo/Markus Schreiber)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Police searched several locations across Berlin overnight and into Sunday, including an apartment in the Schöneberg district. It was not immediately clear where the confrontation happened.
The Associated Press contributed to this report.

title: Wildfires displace more than 250,000 in France, threaten famed wine region
summary: The Gironde fire has burned 162 square miles as 2,500 firefighters and 1,500 soldiers battle the blaze advancing erratically toward Bordeaux.
story: Wildfires are sweeping across Spain and France, forcing more than 250,000 people to evacuate. One blaze is threatening France's famed Bordeaux wine region, while Spain has declared a national emergency. France has deployed the military, and the Tour de France has been shortened as firefighters battle the massive blazes.

More than a quarter-million people have been driven from their homes in southwest France as a massive wildfire barrels toward the famed wine capital of Bordeaux, with officials warning the fast-moving inferno has become so fierce it’s creating its own winds and behaving erratically.

French authorities ordered another 55,000 people to evacuate overnight Sunday from communities south of Bordeaux, bringing the total number of evacuees in the region to about 250,000. Gusty winds, dry conditions and repeated heat waves have fueled a fire that has burned out of control since midweek.
Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said firefighters faced a "difficult" night and warned Sunday that "the situation remains very unfavorable."
EUROPE'S FIRES REVEAL DEADLY MIX OF RECORD HEAT, HUMAN ERROR, ARSON AND LAND MISMANAGEMENT
Firefighters spray water in a burning forest near Lacanau, southwestern France, Saturday, July 25, 2026. (AP Photo/Emma Da Silva)

"The fire again became extremely virulent again and unpredictable, generating its own winds and advancing erratically toward the Bordeaux metropolitan area," Nunez posted on X, adding that the blaze "became calmer by the end of the night."

The fire has now burned an estimated 42,000 hectares, or about 162 square miles — roughly four times the size of Paris — in the Gironde region. Bordeaux Mayor Thomas Cazenave said the flames came within about 9 miles of the city, prompting officials to partially close a major highway into and out of the region.

More than 2,500 firefighters, backed by 18 planes and helicopters, are working to slow the fire's advance. France has also deployed 1,500 soldiers to help clear vegetation and build firebreaks, while several European countries have sent aircraft and firefighting crews to assist.
FRANCE RECORDS MORE THAN 5,700 EXCESS DEATHS DURING HISTORIC EARLY SUMMER HEAT WAVE
Nunez said 450 volunteers have also pitched in to help.

"We ⁠came to lend a hand because if it were our region, we'd want others to do the ​same," 65-year-old farmer Pascal Roudier told Reuters. "And given the scale of the disaster, we ​think our⁠ efforts are very welcome too."
Firefighters battle a wildfire near Marcheprime, outside, Bordeaux, France, Sunday, July 26, 2026. (AP Photo/Emma Da Silva)

The Bordeaux-area fire is one of several major wildfires burning across France. A separate blaze in the neighboring Landes region has forced another 36,000 people to evacuate, while nearly 3,000 others have left their homes in southern France's Var region along the Mediterranean coast.
Neighboring Spain is facing its own wildfire emergency.
A firefighter carries a hose while battling a wildfire in San Martin de Valdeiglesias, west of Madrid, Spain, Sunday, July 26, 2026. (AP Photo/Manu Fernandez)

Authorities there have evacuated about 116,000 people in recent days as fires burned across the Valencia region and west of Madrid. A fast-moving fire in a Valencia suburb killed one man Saturday, marking Spain's first wildfire death in the latest wave of fires.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Earlier this month, 13 people were killed in southern Spain in the country's deadliest wildfire in recent memory.
The Associated Press contributed to this report.

title: South Africa’s illegal migration backlash mirrors political battles across the West
summary: Over 160,000 immigrants have fled as the March and March movement goes house-to-house demanding foreigners leave amid 32.7% unemployment rate.
story: March and March founder and leader Jacinta Ngobese-Zuma says her movement wants illegal immigrants out of the country, calling for tougher action.

JOHANNESBURG: Over 160,000 illegal immigrants have fled South Africa after thousands of citizens took to the streets demanding foreigners leave, as hundreds of thousands of South Africans have followed many in the West in turning against the government for poor border controls, and perceived inaction.

One South African organization claims there are up to 30 million illegal immigrants in a country whose documented citizens number around 63 million. These immigrants, mostly undocumented, are blamed for rampant crime, taking jobs and overrunning hospital wards and places in government schools.

In some cases, groups have gone house-to-house in areas such as Soweto, near Johannesburg, giving deadlines for immigrants to go home. Earlier this month, Reuters reported that 900 people were arrested during a day of nationwide protests. While the protests were largely peaceful, police were called to disperse violent protesters in some areas of the country. One death was reported in the Johannesburg area.
NEW GERMANY SEX-CRIME FIGURES REIGNITE MIGRATION FIGHT AS EXPLOITATION PROBE EXPANDS
Protesters from the March and March movement hold banners and chant slogans during a demonstration in Pinetown, south of Durban, on July 16, 2026. (Rajesh Jantilal/AFP via Getty Images)

Some illegal immigrants have taken buses and left, or been repatriated on flights provided by their home countries across Africa. On one such flight to Ghana in June, the South African border authority said 321 of the 332 Ghanaians who tried to leave Johannesburg’s OR Tambo International Airport were found to be in the country illegally.

Up to five immigrants have been killed by protesters so far this year, but the most prominent anti-immigrant civic group in South Africa, the March and March movement, claims that it is against violence. It is their followers who march the country’s streets, often with large traditional sticks called knobkerries, "encouraging" foreigners to leave.

Their founder and leader, Jacinta Ngobese-Zuma, told Fox News Digital, "We’ve had enough," claiming the number of illegal immigrants living in South Africa is "between 15 and 30 million, and that's an arguable number because everyone is always debating what the actual number is."

Undocumented migrants line up near a bus at the Durban Drive In in Durban, on June 29, 2026, preparing to leave before the camp will shut down and the operation will be transferred to the border with Zimbabwe. South Africans President Cyril Ramaphosa vowed on June 25 to crush any attempts to destabilize the nation during planned anti-immigrant marches next week, amid a wave of xenophobia.  (Marco Longari/AFP via Getty Images)

The number 30 million is contentious. The only official published figures are from a census taken in 2022 by Statistics SA, queried by some critics because the organization is controlled by the ANC government, under attack for reportedly causing the illegal immigration crisis and therefore seen to be benefiting from low statistics. The body claims there are up to 3 million immigrants in the country, but Ngobese-Zuma points out this figure includes people who have documents "they're just using the numbers from those who were admitted to being in the country legally."

Immigrants have frequently been seen running away when requested by officials, including Stats SA officials, to show their documents. The head of Statistics SA, Risenga Maluleke, even admitted to the local Eyewitness News that his officials don’t check information on the occasions that they can find immigrants, saying "when people say I was born outside South Africa, we take what they say because we have not had a way of proving it other than relying on what they say."
Protesters start a fire in the streets of Johannesburg, South Africa, on June 30, 2026. (Reuters)

Ngobese-Zuma added, "The country is being invaded, and we decided to do something about it. There's too much crime going on at the hands of foreign nationals. The actual truth is that a lot of them go unfound because nobody knows who they are. They're not on record. Their fingerprints are not on the system. So there [are] a lot of cases actually that are outstanding when it comes to the issue of illegal immigrants."

Statistics South Africa recently reported that the official unemployment rate for the country is 32.7%. Yet almost all illegal immigrants have found work here, with the country’s president, Cyril Ramaphosa, admitting to the nation in a televised address last month, "Some employers hire undocumented immigrants because they pay them wages that are well below the minimum wage and make them work longer hours without due compensation."
DHS ISSUES $84B IN FINES TO ILLEGAL IMMIGRANTS UNDER TRUMP ADMINISTRATION

This led March and March’s Ngobese-Zuma to say, "The issue of jobs is also very important. In our community, where there's the highest unemployment in the world, it only makes sense that South Africans are out there demanding that they be prioritized when it comes to employment."

Several reports claim that in a local Johannesburg government hospital, built to offer practically free care to South Africa’s citizens, patients, even in the ER, have to wait up to 36 hours to be seen, because so many foreigners come to the hospital and use the facilities. At least one patient has died waiting to be seen at the Helen Joseph hospital, near to the center of the city.
March and March leader Jacinta Ngobese-Zuma leads a demonstration in Mtwalume, south of Durban, on July 9, 2026. (Rajesh Jantilal/AFP via Getty Iamges)

Ngobese-Zuma pointed out, "We have a welfare (health and education) system in the country, and currently people are flocking in from all over the African continent and the world to come and take advantage of these free things that they think are free when it's actually taxpayers that are paying for it."

Border controls are so lax that it’s said hundreds of thousands have simply waded across low rivers in some cases to enter South Africa, with crocodiles a bigger problem than police or immigration officials. Bribery and corruption at border posts is endemic. But following the public outcry, and perhaps significantly with local elections coming up, President Ramaphosa has now vowed to "crack down" on immigration issues. As of July 11, the government claims a total of 53,449 foreign nationals have been processed for deportation and repatriation.

This represents less than 0.2% of the illegal immigrants said to be in the country by March and March. Public pressure groups, and politicians such as Herman Mashaba, are calling on the government to do much, much more. Mashaba is president of Action SA, a small but campaigning party in South Africa’s parliament that has been battling illegal immigration for 10 years.

Mashaba told Fox News Digital, "Action SA is deeply frustrated by the government's weak and reactionary response to South Africa's immigration crisis, which is ultimately the consequence of three decades of ANC (the ruling party) failure to secure our borders,"
MISSOURI SENATOR WARNS DEM IMMIGRATION POLICIES THREATEN WESTERN CIVILIZATION AFTER SCORING ICE FUNDING WIN

Anti-immigrant marchers walk through the streets of Johannesburg on the day of an unofficial deadline set by anti-immigrant groups for all undocumented migrants to leave, in Johannesburg, South Africa, June 30, 2026. (Reuters/Oupa Nkosi)

"Rather than presenting a meaningful shift in approach, which we believe must center on mass deportations and the urgent strengthening of immigration enforcement capacity, the government appears determined to simply repackage the same failed and outdated policies that have done nothing to address the consequences of weak border controls and chronic underinvestment in enforcing our immigration laws."

"As in Europe, South Africans have turned against their government on immigration policy," analyst Frans Cronje told Fox News Digital. Cronje, president of the Washington-based Yorktown Foundation for Freedom, added, "Polls conducted earlier this year ranked immigration as the second most pressing concern from South Africans behind unemployment. Overall, 23% of South Africans cited unemployment as the most pressing issue for the government to address, followed by 11.7% who cited immigration, 10.1% who cited corruption and 9.8% who cited crime."

Cronje continued, "Black South Africans (82% of the population) were three times as likely as their White counterparts to see immigration as a problem for the government to address. Hostility toward immigrants runs very high with regular protest marches and threats and intimidation directed at immigrant communities who are accused of taking jobs and businesses from South Africans, and driving high levels of crime".
South African President Cyril Ramaphosa delivers the State of the Nation address in Cape Town, South Africa, on Feb. 12, 2026. (Rodger Bosch/Pool via Reuters)

Responding when asked why activists such as March and March are taking action, Ngobese-Zuma said, "It's the government that should be the one that's making sure that when people say that they don't want certain people in their communities, they remove them before the communities remove them themselves. I think the government is complacent about not only the issue of immigration, our government is just complacent about a lot of things, especially that have to do with crime."
Protests against immigrants have turned nasty in previous years. Sixty-two were killed in riots in 2008, and at least five in 2015.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Ngobese-Zuma agrees March and March members are gatvol – Afrikaans slang, politely put to mean completely fed up – telling Fox News Digital, "We don't care which country comes forward and tells us that we are xenophobic. We've had enough, and nobody can tell us that we must now accept people staying in our country illegally."
Fox News Digital reached out to the South African government, but did not receive a response.
Paul Tilsley is a veteran correspondent who has reported from four continents for more than three decades. Based in Johannesburg, South Africa, he can be followed on X @paultilsley.

title: At least 1 dead, several injured after van rams into crowd at Pride festival; suspect 'known to police'
summary: A van rammed into the Christopher Street Day festival in Berlin's Tiergarten, killing one person, and police launched an intensive manhunt and later identified a suspect with alleged Islamic ties.
story: Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.
German authorities on Saturday canceled a popular Pride festival after one person was killed, and numerous others were injured, when a van rammed into a crowd in Berlin.
Police said there are at least 16 people injured who were treated by rescue personnel.
The incident occurred during the European city's annual Christopher Street Day festival, an LGBTQ+ Pride event.
In an ongoing manhunt for a suspect, Berlin police said they had identified a person who has not been arrested and has alleged ties to Islamic groups, The Associated Press reported.

"The suspect is known to police. He is known to us as a member of Islamic circles here in Berlin, and our search for this person is proceeding at full speed," said police spokesman Florian Nath. "We still have no information whatsoever regarding his specific motives, the exact sequence of events, or his role in the crime itself."
GUNFIRE SHATTERS TORONTO LATIN STREET FESTIVAL, LEAVING AT LEAST 2 DEAD AND MULTIPLE WOUNDED
Police officers were on the scene after the cancellation of Christopher Street Day in Berlin Saturday. (Fabian Sommer/DPA via AP)
"We are conducting an intensive manhunt for suspects," police added, later clarifying that there could be one or more suspects.

"At this point, we don’t know anything about possible motives, the identity of the perpetrator or the perpetrators, or anything of that nature," Police spokesperson Alexander Klute told The Associated Press.

By three in the morning local time, police had detained someone whom they said is involved with the "Islamist scene in Berlin," Berlin broadcaster Deutsche Welle reported, adding that it's unclear if the man drove the van.
Emergency personnel gather in Berlin after the cancellation of Christopher Street Day festivities.  (AP Photo/Markus Schreiber)
After the van plowed into the crowd it hit a tree, police said.
More than 2,000 officers have been protecting the event since it started Saturday morning.
In an update, the police said several of the injuries are life-threatening.
Crowds at the Christopher Street Day festival in Berlin, which was canceled after police say several people were injured when a van rammed the festivities Saturday. (Fabian Sommer/DPA via AP)
Hundreds of thousands of people turned out for the event, which included a parade and ended Saturday evening with a show at Tiergarten park near Brandenberg Gate.
Emergency personnel gather following the cancellation of Christopher Street Day festivities in Berlin, on Saturday. (AP Photo/Markus Schreiber)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"It is an attack on our free and open society — after a peaceful and colorful CSD, the assembly for a tolerant and peaceful Berlin was attacked in the most brutal way," Berlin Mayor Kai Wegner said in a translated X post. "Berlin is the city of freedom — and our freedom has been attacked in the most horrific way today.

"My thoughts are with the victims, their families and friends. I thank the emergency services who were immediately on site and did everything in their power. And I trust the police and security authorities, who will investigate at full speed."
Brie Stimson is a Los Angeles-based entertainment and breaking news writer for Fox News Digital.

title: Francesca Hong avoids attacks as Wisconsin Democrats meet for governor debate
summary: The five Democratic candidates for governor in Wisconsin almost entirely refrained from lobbing attacks at one another during their only debate Tuesday night, even as the volatile race enters its final two weeks.
story: The five Democratic candidates for governor in Wisconsin almost entirely refrained from lobbing attacks at one another during their only debate Tuesday night, even as the volatile race enters its final two weeks.

With early voting underway ahead of the high-stakes Aug. 11 primary — and with a huge chunk of Democratic voters still undecided — no one onstage took a direct swing at polling front-runner Francesca Hong, a state representative from Madison and democratic socialist, despite growing concerns from some in the party about her viability in a general election.

The only tense moment of the hourlong debate came between Hong’s top two rivals for the nomination. Former Lt. Gov. Mandela Barnes jabbed Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley for re-entering the race this month with outgoing Gov. Tony Evers’ endorsement after Lt. Gov. Sara Rodriguez abruptly dropped out.

“It’s been mentioned that the county executive had his campaign resurrected by special interests in a dark room with people with their thumb on the scale,” Barnes said. “Things will always be the same with that sort of leadership. We should be asking for more.”
Crowley didn’t directly respond, but at another moment, he said that “I was actually born into struggle” and that “I’m not here to protect the establishment.”

Otherwise, the three candidates, along with state Sen. Kelda Roys and Joel Brennan, former secretary of the Department of Administration, expressed near-total agreement on a variety of issues, including lowering property taxes, scaling back a school voucher program and taxing people earning more than $1 million annually.

Not even Hong’s affiliation with the Democratic Socialists of America emerged as a point of controversy from her competitors, even as Democrats have increasingly expressed fear that she would be too far to the left to defeat Rep. Tom Tiffany, the likely Republican nominee, in November in the swing state.
Hong has faced criticism over the course of the campaign for her past calls to defund and abolish the police and her opinion that a “perfect world would be a world without prisons.”
Asked about those comments by the debate moderators Tuesday, as well as whether she agreed with other controversial positions touted by the national DSA, Hong softened her stance.

“I do not support the full platform of the national DSA, and I am not endorsed by DSA national. What democratic socialism is is a form of government that puts working-class people first,” she said, before she reiterated her support for stronger public education funding, taxing the rich and investing in universal childcare and affordable housing.
“I am looking forward to helping the Democrats become the big-tent party that they’ve aimed to be for many years,” she added.
At another point, during a discussion about whether wealthy Wisconsinites would flee the state if they were taxed more, Hong expressed hope that they, too, could benefit from her proposed policies.
“We can improve the quality of life for millionaires and ensure that they, too, will be able to live, work and thrive here in our state,” she said.

And during a part of the debate focused on the fatal shooting of a Madison man by a police officer last week — which led to protests and demands for accountability — Hong backed off from her previous statements supporting cutting funding for police departments.
Asked whether she would sign a bill or a budget that cut police funding, Hong, who just last week dubbed the shooting an “execution,” replied, “No.”
“The governor cannot defund police, and I’m not here to govern by slogan. I’m here to make sure that I am the governor that is most serious about public safety,” she said.
It was one of several areas of agreement among the candidates.

Barnes said, “We should all be very disturbed by what we saw in those images, what we saw in the video, and we should fight as hard as we possibly can, as a state, as a people, as a society, to make sure that never happens again.” But, he said, “of course, I would not sign a budget that reduced funding” for police.
Crowley said that “it’s extremely important that we have transparency” but that “we cannot defund the police.”

Meanwhile, Barnes, the former lieutenant governor who narrowly lost the 2022 Senate race in Wisconsin, at times attempted to make an electability argument, touting himself as the “only person onstage who’s actually won statewide.”

In his closing statement, Barnes pointed to a Marquette University Law School poll last week that showed him beating Tiffany in a hypothetical matchup. He also said the “establishment was trying to rig this election” for their preferred candidate while noting that Republicans were meddling in the Democratic primary to boost the person they want to face in November. While he did not name them, those lines were in reference to Crowley and Hong, respectively.
Crowley tried to differentiate himself by arguing that none of his Democratic opponents “have actually run local government” like he has.

At the start of the debate, Crowley was also asked whether voters should trust his judgment after NBC News reported last week on the existence of a years-old social media account registered to him that featured incendiary posts about women and race, along with derogatory LGBTQ references.

“I’m here to deliver real results for Wisconsinites all over our state,” Crowley said before he nodded to his endorsement from Evers and “labor unions and leaders all across this state who believe in my leadership.”

title: Fed interest rate vote poses a test for Warsh as Iran war, tariff push send prices higher
summary: Inflation and affordability are top issues for the Federal Reserve’s rate-setting committee as it votes on whether to raise interest rates or keep them steady.
story: The debate over the best course for interest rates continued to swirl heading into Wednesday’s rate-setting vote at the Federal Reserve in Washington.

While parts of the U.S. economy are relatively stable, like the labor market, experts say this stability could be undermined by the potential inflationary impacts of a longer Iran war or the Trump administration’s latest tariff push.

Interest rate traders believe the Federal Open Market Committee will keep its Fed Funds Rate, which sets many other borrowing rates throughout the economy, at its current level of about 3.6%, where it has been since December.
While the consensus is for a rate hold, there is an outside possibility that the vote could result in the FOMC recommending a rate hike.

For many consumers and smaller businesses, current interest rates have already pushed the cost of borrowing money increasingly out of reach. This has cut into sales of items like autos and industrial equipment, which are typically financed.

At the same time, the inflation rate has hovered above the Fed’s 2% target for more than five years, a phenomenon that has exacerbated an ongoing affordability crisis. And while some recent inflation indicators have begun showing declines, the pace of rising prices for energy and wholesale items has remained elevated.

“Every month of above-target inflation has compounded the strain on Americans’ budgets,” Dallas Federal Reserve President Lorie Logan said in remarks earlier this month, calling for rates to be “modestly” higher.

The Fed has historically raised rates to curb overall economic activity and rein in inflation. With inflation stubbornly high, many market participants have called for higher rates that would put downward pressure on the pace of price increases.

Among interest rate traders, there is a broad consensus that the Fed will raise rates before the end of the year. According to CME FedWatch, Fed Funds futures contracts point to a 90% probability that rates will be at least 0.25% higher by January.
There is another question hanging over the central bank’s rate-setting meeting this week: How much of an impact would raising interest rates actually have on prices?
Currently, there are several reasons why inflation could potentially be less sensitive to higher interest rates than it has in the past.

High energy prices sparked by the war with Iran, for example, and Trump administration tariff policies are both helping to keep prices elevated for consumers. But experts say higher rates would do little to blunt these kinds of geopolitical forces.
“Hiking [interest rates] doesn’t open up the Strait of Hormuz or end the war,” said Adam Turnquist, chief technical strategist at the asset management group LPL Financial.
The opinions of the Fed’s leaders as to what lies ahead for the U.S. economy will likely also be more of a black box this week than they have been in recent years.

Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh, who took the reins of the central bank from Jerome Powell in May, has made it a hallmark of his tenure not to tip the Fed’s thinking about the path of monetary policy — much to the frustration of some market participants.
“Chair Warsh’s communication void has encouraged other policymakers to speak more forcefully,” said Greg Daco, chief economist at EY-Parthenon, Ernst & Young LLP.
Among those who speak up, the message has been consistent, Daco wrote in a note: Inflation remains too high and rates must increase.

“After months of upside inflation surprises, patience is wearing thin,” wrote Daco. “If inflation does not soon move back toward 2%, and remains elevated because of persistent supply shocks, stronger AI-related demand, tariffs, or the Middle East conflict, the case for additional policy firming will be clear.”
Other experts are more optimistic that inflation has peaked and  the Fed can afford to keep rates at current levels.

“Housing-related inflation continues to cool, and wage growth—the largest input cost in services — is not inflationary when adjusted for productivity gains,” Angelo Kourkafas, a senior investment strategist at Edward Jones, wrote in a recent client note.
“Moreover, the new tariffs announced are broadly consistent with the previous tariff levels that expired and should not trigger a renewed rise in goods prices,” he added.
President Donald Trump’s latest tariffs — a blanket rate of between 10% and 12.5% on dozens of U.S. trade partners — represent a continuation of his protectionist trade policies.

But they also introduce fresh uncertainty into many of America’s  most vital economic relationships. Several of the targeted trade partners say the U.S. rationale for this round of import duties — an effort to combat forced labor — amounts to a false pretense.
Within days of their announcement, the latest tariffs were challenged in federal trade court, effectively throwing them into legal limbo even as importers prepare to start paying them.
Some experts believe the tariffs are unlikely to survive a legal challenge, adding yet another layer of uncertainty to the economic outlook.

title: BTS say they will not submit their music to the Grammy Awards
summary: K-pop band BTS said that they will not submit their music for consideration at the 2027 Grammy Awards, citing concerns over category divisions.
story: K-pop sensation BTS said Wednesday that it will not submit its music for consideration at the 2027 Grammy Awards, citing concerns over category divisions.
The seven members — RM, Jimin, V, Suga, Jungkook, Jin and J-Hope — uploaded the same statement to their individual Instagram accounts.
“We have decided not to enter the Grammys this year,” a translation of the message read. “I hope that music can be heard and loved for what it is, rather than being divided by region or language.”
The Recording Academy did not immediately return a request for comment.

The hugely popular BTS group was widely expected to be nominated for some of the Recording Academy’s top awards at the 69th Grammy Awards — including album of the year. The South Korean boyband’s most recent album “Arirang” has been one of the best-selling records of the year.
Arirang’s lead single “Swim” was a Billboard Hot 100 No. 1 hit in the United States.

Under the new categorizations, the band’s song “Swim” might have been excluded from competing for best Asian pop music performance at the awards, one of the five new categories the Recording Academy announced last month. The new awards were sold as an effort to boost inclusivity.

While a lot of BTS’ songs are in Korean, the lead track is mostly sung in English. A rulebook for the Grammy Awards specifies that the recordings for the new award “must feature meaningful use of one or more Asian languages.”
“An Asian language should play a significant role within the song in bilingual or multilingual structures such that the recording is identifiable with that language,” the rulebook reads.

BTS, which formed in 2013 and has been compared to The Beatles, has previously performed at the award show and was the first K-pop act to receive a Grammy nomination - earning five nominations but so far winning none.

BTS stands for the Korean phrase “Bangtan Sonyeondan,” which translates to “Bulletproof Boy Scouts.” The band has a huge global following and recently performed in the United States during the World Cup final’s halftime show.
On Wednesday, the group thanked its fans for their support.
“Thank you to Army and everyone who is always with us,” the band said.

title: Anthony Fauci invokes Fifth Amendment right not to testify at Covid hearing
summary: Dr. Anthony Fauci declined to answer senators’ questions at a hearing Wednesday on the origins of Covid and the government’s handling of the pandemic, saying he would invoke his Fifth Amendment right to avoid the possibility that Republicans could try to use his testimony to prosecute him for perjury.
story: Dr. Anthony Fauci declined to answer senators’ questions at a hearing Wednesday on the origins of Covid and the government’s handling of the pandemic, saying he would invoke his Fifth Amendment right to avoid the possibility that Republicans could try to use his testimony to prosecute him for perjury.
The surprise decision shook up the hearing, which was expected to be contentious given Fauci’s previous public clashes with Chairman Rand Paul, R-Ky.

In his opening statement to the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee, Fauci pointed to Paul’s “obvious obsession with calling for my prosecution, his repeated slanderous comments about me” and his decision to publicly release the doctor’s personal journal.

“The only conclusion I can reach is that the sole reason he is calling me before this committee is to get me to say something — anything — that could vindicate his repeated public pledges that I end up, in his words — quote — ‘behind bars,’” Fauci said.

“Any reasonable person who has followed his unhinged obsession with me would readily come to the same conclusion,” he continued. “Therefore, although it pains me to do so because of the respect I have for the legislative branch of government and my decades-long record of cooperating with Congress, under the advice of my attorneys, I will invoke my right under the 5th Amendment of the Constitution to refrain from answering your questions.”

Fauci also pointed to his previous appearances before House and Senate committees. He said in his opening remarks that during the nearly 40 years that he served as the director of the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases, he testified before or briefed congressional committees “well over 200 times.” During his tenure, he said he “proved that I believe in and respect the value of legitimate congressional oversight.”
Despite Fauci’s refusal to respond, Paul still used his time at the hearing to ask the doctor a series of questions.
Fauci answered each question with the same line: “On the advice of counsel, I respectfully decline to answer based upon my rights under the 5th Amendment to the Constitution.”
At the end of his questioning, Paul told Fauci that he would face “repercussions” for not answering questions.

“The committee will have to consider after this hearing what appropriate action should be taken against you for the failure to testify after being directed to do so,” Paul said. “It’s against the law to obstruct an investigation of Congress. There will be repercussions to your refusal to testify today.”

When Paul concluded, Fauci’s attorney tried to say something to the lawmakers. He was repeatedly cut off by Paul, who said he was not recognized to speak. Moments later, Paul ordered security to remove Fauci’s lawyer from the committee room.
Shortly after Fauci’s lawyer left the hearing, he told NBC News that Fauci “has a valid Fifth Amendment privilege, and he has the right to assert it.”
“That’s what I was trying to tell the committee, and that’s all I was trying to tell the committee,” the lawyer said.
The top Democrat on the committee, Sen. Gary Peters, D-Mich., slammed the Republicans’ handling of the hearing, saying in his period of questioning that he believed the hearing “does real damage.”

“It’s tempting to turn one person into the scapegoat for a crisis that hundreds of officials across both the Trump and the Biden administration were responsible for handling,” Peters said, adding that people were facing death threats.
“This is only going to, unfortunately, deter other scientific experts from public service to understand that this is what they would have to go through as they provide their advice to us,” he added.
Separately, Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., told reporters that he would not ask Fauci questions during his allotted time to speak.
“This show trial is a perjury craft for criminal prosecution going forward,” Blumenthal said, calling Fauci’s decision to exercise his Fifth Amendment right “the more prudent course.”
Instead, Blumenthal used his period of time to defend Fauci and criticize Republicans’ handling of both the hearing and health issues facing the country.

“Put aside all the flowery rhetoric that we hear in the United States Senate,” he said. “Dr. Fauci has saved lives, as have public health officials in the United States and throughout the world. And today, we are demeaning and degrading their lifesaving service.”

Ahead of the hearing, Paul pointed to the possibility of Fauci facing prosecution for perjury if he lied to Congress. Paul has previously alleged that Fauci has lied to Congress, an allegation that Fauci has denied.
On Tuesday, Paul responded to a reporter’s question about how he would respond to people who argue that the senator was trying to put Fauci in a position to perjure himself.

“There’s no risk to perjury if you tell the truth,” Paul said. “In fact, he can even admit to not telling the truth in the past. He can admit destroying records. He can admit to, you know not adequately presenting both sides of equations, which isn’t really a crime. He can admit to anything. The only thing he can’t do is lie again.”

Former President Joe Biden issued a preemptive pardon for Fauci in the final hours of his administration. Fauci responded at the time by saying that he had been “the subject of politically motivated threats of investigation and prosecution.” The doctor said he “committed no crime.”

Responding to a question earlier this week about whether he believed Fauci should face prosecution, Paul said, “I think there are a couple of questions,” adding that “we’re going to find out” at the hearing. Paul referenced Fauci’s pardon and expressed the possibility that it could be challenged.
“Whether that will be challenged, I don’t know,” Paul said.
Fauci’s lawyer, David Schertler, said in a statement that the circumstances surrounding Fauci’s appearance “regrettably made his continued cooperation impossible.”

Schertler said Paul has had “an intense and seemingly pathological course of retribution, revenge, and obsession with Dr. Fauci,” which has ultimately led to Fauci and his family facing threats and harassment.

“Dr. Fauci devoted his lengthy career to saving millions of lives globally through scientific discovery and sound public health policy,” Schertler said in the statement. “The accusations that Chairman Paul continues to propagate are false and disgraceful, and we will examine all options to hold him accountable.”
Ahead of the hearing, Paul told reporters that he thinks Americans “would be very disappointed” if Fauci invoked his Fifth Amendment privileges.

title: At least 13 killed in Japan earthquake as rescuers search for survivors in a ‘race against time’
summary: At least 13 people have been killed in southwestern Japan after a magnitude-7.1 earthquake, Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi said Wednesday, as rescuers searched for people trapped in collapsed buildings including a shopping mall.
story: At least 13 people have been killed in southwestern Japan after a magnitude-7.1 earthquake, Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi said Wednesday, as rescuers searched for people trapped in collapsed buildings including a shopping mall.

“Even now, there are people waiting to be rescued, and this is a race against time. We will marshal all available resources on the ground to save and rescue as many people as possible,” Takaichi told reporters in Tokyo.

The quake struck Tuesday afternoon in Kumamoto prefecture on Japan’s southern main island of Kyushu at a relatively shallow depth of 6 miles, prompting tsunami warnings and evacuation from coastal areas. The epicenter was about 12 miles south of the city of Kumamoto, which has a population of about 700,000.

While the tsunami warning was lifted shortly after, the quake caused extensive damage throughout the prefecture, including to historic buildings such as Kumamoto Castle, a popular tourist site that is still under repair from another deadly quake in the same area in 2016.
It also ruptured roads and left thousands of homes without power, with officials warning residents to beware of heat stroke as temperatures reach well into the 90s.

title: Trump reportedly issues menacing new threat after Iran targets U.S. forces in thwarted missile attack
summary: The fighting shattered a brief period of calm after weeks of escalation between the U.S. and Iran over the strategic Strait of Hormuz.
story: President Donald Trump vowed to “beat the f***ing s*** out of” Iran after Tehran launched an attack on American forces in the Middle East, Fox News reported Wednesday.
“They’re going to get a beating,” Trump said, according to Fox’s chief foreign correspondent Trey Yingst.

The comments followed what the U.S. described as a “surprise attack,” which prompted Saudi Arabia and the United States to retaliate against a Tehran-backed militia in Iraq and shatter a period of relative calm raising the risk of a further escalation of the conflict.

Iran had suspended its attacks amid a renewed push to reach a deal with the U.S., but warned earlier this week that it would not allow Washington to dictate the “timing of war and peace,” while maintaining that the Strait of Hormuz was “closed.”
The sudden return of hostilities shattered the relative calm that had descended on Iran for several days after the U.S. paused daily strikes on the Islamic Republic in order to make room for peace

Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said it had launched strikes on a U.S. air base and military central command center in Jordan, state-run Nour News agency reported early Wednesday, local time. Its navy also struck three oil tankers that it said were “in violation” of its blockade of the Strait off Hormuz, according to the state-run news agency IRNA.

In a post on X, U.S. Central Command, or CENTCOM, said it had thwarted an “attempted surprise attack” on forces based in the Middle East around 5.45 p.m. Tuesday. All Iranian missiles were successfully intercepted, it said, but troops remained “vigilant and at a high state of readiness.”

Just hours later, CENTCOM said it had launched “precision strikes” in Iraq alongside the Saudi armed forces against “Iran-aligned terrorists” that it said the IRGC had directed to attack U.S. forces and Saudi energy infrastructure.

title: James Comey legal team argues DOJ’s seashells case erodes ‘bedrock’ principles
summary: It’s the second time the Trump administration has found a way to criminally charge the former FBI director, whom Trump has targeted for years.
story: Allowing the seashells-based prosecution of former FBI Director James Comey to move forward would erode core constitutional rights protecting free speech, Comey’s legal team told a federal judge in North Carolina on Tuesday.

On Tuesday, members of Comey’s eight-person legal team filed a motion asking a judge to toss the seashells case, saying it is “not based on a good-faith application of the law to the facts; instead, it effectuates a yearslong campaign by the President to use the criminal process to punish Mr. Comey for his protected speech and because of the President’s deep-seated animosity.”

The Trump-driven case must be cast aside “under two bedrock legal doctrines,” they said: that the case was instigated based on Comey’s protected speech and that the government engaged in selective prosecution.

“Dismissal of federal criminal charges under these doctrines has historically been rare. That is because for decades the DOJ’s independence and integrity have guarded against the use of the criminal process to punish enemies or settle political scores,” they wrote. “The prosecutions of Mr. Comey mark a sharp break from that tradition.”

Comey’s team also filed a separate motion Tuesday seeking the disclosure of grand jury records in the case, arguing that while “grand jury proceedings are typically entitled to a presumption of regularity, the irregularities surrounding the return of the indictment in this case overcome that presumption.”

Comey’s team had already argued Monday that the seashells case should be tossed because Comey’s Instagram post was not a true threat, arguing that “dictionaries, context, precedent, and common sense” gut the Trump administration’s claims about the meaning of the numbers “8647.”

A Justice Department official who was not authorized to discuss the case previously told NBC News that the case was a “complete loser” and a “waste of resources” and predicted that it would be tossed before trial. “No reasonable person could believe that Comey intended to threaten the president via seashells,” the person said. “Everyone at this DOJ should be ashamed. I know I am.”
U.S. District Judge Louise Flanagan is overseeing the case. If the case survives to trial, Comey would be arraigned Sept. 30, and the trial would take place Oct. 21 in New Bern, North Carolina.

Matthew Petracca, a rookie federal prosecutor and former Republican official in New Jersey, brought the case under the U.S. attorney for the Eastern District of North Carolina, W. Ellis Boyle, a Trump administration appointee, but he dropped off the case in late May.
In one of their motions, Comey’s lawyers note that Petracca became an actual assistant U.S. attorney on April 26, just two days before the Comey case was brought.

“We note that Mr. Petracca was at all times professional in his interaction with the defense team,” Comey’s attorneys wrote. “We only note his limited experience in that it is unusual in most circumstances for such a high-profile case to be delegated to a junior attorney.”

Petracca, they write, had a “background in state Medicaid fraud and little federal criminal experience” and has since “withdrawn from the case and transferred to the Civil Division.” Assistant U.S. Attorney Timothy Severo is now heading the prosecution.

Comey’s team made a similar argument of vindictiveness and selective prosecution after former White House aide Lindsey Halligan brought a case against him over testimony he gave in 2020. Included in that filing was a 60-page list of statements that Trump made about Comey from May 2017 to the fall of 2025.

But a judge never ruled on the arguments of vindictiveness and selective prosecution in that case, instead finding the entire case was invalid because Halligan could not legally hold the position she claimed.

title: The best editor-approved meat delivery services in 2026
summary: We tested steak, chicken, seafood and more from brands like Omaha Steaks, Butcherbox, and Lobsterboys to see which has the best meat delivery service for your next BBQ.
story: Summertime is grilling season, and gone are the days when you have to schlep to the supermarket through Saturday morning heat to get the best pick of cuts. Meat delivery services offer a reliable, convenient alternative to buying in-store, often with access to types and cuts of meat that you may not find at your local grocery. I spoke to Coco Pierrel, certified integrative nutritionist and founder of Eat Shed Glow, as well as Dr. Susan Kais, a dual board-certified gastroenterologist and IBD specialist at UC Health, to find out more about picking the best meat delivery service before your next BBQ.

Butcherbox uses a subscription-based model that allows you to choose from their full selection of meat and seafood, which includes over 80 core and specialty cuts, according to the brand. The subscription allows for a choice of a medium, large or extra-large box with your choice of proteins, with prices ranging from $179 to $319 per box. You can also choose how often your box is delivered depending on your cooking needs.

Although the offerings include chicken breast, shrimp, salmon and more, the star of the show is definitely the beef. The brand has a wide range of beef options, including grass-fed, pasture-raised, grain-finished, free-range and more. The meat is sourced in the US, aside from the grass-fed and grass-finished cuts, which are from Australia due to its ideal grassland climate, according to the brand.

I received an assortment of beef, chicken and seafood from the brand, including my favorite, the sockeye salmon. It was juicy, tender and one of the meatiest salmon I’ve ever tried — it was thick, firm and had the telltale bright pink hue of high-quality salmon. I also like that the products came in smaller packages, rather than boxes, which makes them easier to maneuver around your freezer, and I also noticed how well the dry ice packs held up, even in the summer heat. After unpacking the meat, the ice was still cold in the box hours later — my roommate even ended up using it as a coolant for making some homemade ice cream.

If you’re looking to order a full family meal, Omaha Steaks is your best bet. The brand sent me an assortment of meats, including beef tenderloin, filet mignons and strip steak, all of which I enjoyed. However, what really drives it home are the sides. Alongside the meat, I also received frozen scallop potatoes and desserts like caramel apple tartelets and chocolate lava cake. I love the all-in-one approach the brand takes, since it takes away the hassle of deciding on side dishes — although I personally love dreaming up sides, this is probably really convenient for those who may be in a rush to cook, or more on the indecisive side. The brand’s wide selection also extends to its pricing — you can find selections for as little as $10, along with deals on bigger boxes and customizable bulk options.

The food arrived in separately packaged boxes, inside of a box filled with dry ice and freezer bags to keep everything cold and frozen. Inside of each box, the meat and desserts were also individually packaged, which I appreciated since it made everything easier to separate for meal prepping and helped to save space in the freezer.

Of the meats, my favorite is the strip steak, which I love using to make quick and simple steak meals for weeknight dinners. The steak was juicy and tender, which speaks to how well it was frozen since the texture wasn’t compromised at all. I also like the preparation instructions for each type of meat on the brand’s website (which, after accidentally reducing a wagyu burger to little more than a burnt disc, I highly recommend following).

You can choose between beef, pork, chicken, lamb and seafood products, along with market items like beef tallow, wood chunks for smoking and grilling, BBQ tool sets and more. A la carte options include sirloin filets for as little as $14, with the most expensive steak cut, the tomahawk ribeye, priced at $135. You can also choose from a selection of curated boxes, or build your own for a personalized touch.

How to choose a meat delivery service

The first factor you’ll want to consider is the type of meat offered. While various services specialize in specific types — for example, Omaha Steaks is known for its high-quality cuts of steak and beef — many offer a range of beef, poultry, pork and even seafood. That being said, your personal preference is most important in this case, so you’ll want to look for a service that specializes in your favorite types, or at least has a wide enough selection that you’ll be able to find the cuts you’re looking for.

According to Pierrel, two non-negotiables for raising meat are avoiding antibiotics and added hormones. Adding hormones is banned in chicken but still legal in beef, so Pierrel suggests checking for third-party verification, like the USDA Process Verified shield, which shows that a brand’s processes have been independently audited by the USDA.

She also says it’s important to understand these various certifications. “Words like ‘premium’, ‘natural,’ and ‘butcher’s cut’ have no legal definition; they just sound official,” she says. However, there are a few terms she suggests keeping an eye out for when looking at how your meat was raised.

Grass-fed and pasture-raised labels are great to look for if your budget allows it (since they tend to be a bit pricier). While grass-fed tells you what an animal ate, pasture-raised ensures the animal lived unconfined, outside of the grazing area, says Pierrel. “That combination produces meat that’s more nutrient-dense per bite, with a higher omega-3 profile, so it satisfies you with less,” she says. For an insider tip, she recommends looking for grass-finished meat as well, since it guarantees grass for life, unlike the grass-fed labeling.USDA Organic is the federally inspected certification that guarantees the meat has been fed organically, with no pesticides, antibiotics or added hormones, and real access to pastures, says Pierrel. However, since the certification process can be expensive, a lot of high-quality, smaller farms may skip the process. You can still vet their sourcing by looking at their listed farm suppliers, which Pierrel says is a good test of transparency. “A company proud of its sourcing names its farms,” she says.As of January 2026, Product of USA is a label that requires the animal to be born, raised and processed fully in the United States, says Pierrel. “Since most grass-fed beef sold here is imported, that one label now lets your grocery money support American farmers doing it right,” she says.

There are pros and cons to both fresh and frozen meat, according to the experts. The choice will ultimately depend on your personal preferences and uses for the meat.

Fresh meat is great for meals you’ll be preparing right away or in the days soon after your delivery. Usually, being able to cook the meat right away will result in a better texture and flavor, says Kais. However, since it has a shorter shelf life, it needs to be enjoyed quickly. Fresh meat also ages through transit, whereas frozen meat is flash frozen right after processing, which preserves it at its peak, says Pierrel.Frozen meat is an excellent alternative to fresh, especially from a nutritional and safety standpoint. The flash-freezing not only helps preserve quality and nutrients, but reduces the risk of spoilage during transit as well, says Kais. Pierrel says it’s also “the smarter way to stock up”, since you can save it for later in your freezer, while Kais adds that it often also provides more selection, since specialty cuts may not be available fresh. The only con is that frozen meats can sometimes experience changes in texture after thawing; however, Kais says that it shouldn’t be a major issue if handled properly (and in my experience, I had no issues with texture).

Fresh meat needs to arrive at your door below 40 degrees Fahrenheit, since bacteria develop fastest in what the USDA calls the Danger Zone, which is between 40 degrees and 140 degrees Fahrenheit, says Pierrel. Beef in the US is graded by the USDA, and primarily focuses on marbling, which is the intramuscular fat that’s woven inside of the muscle, according to experts. “Marbling is important because it melts during cooking, helping keep the meat more tender and flavorful,” says Kais. However, Pierrel says that many shoppers aren’t aware of exactly how the grading is assessed. “The grade is assessed on the ribeye, between the 12th and 13th ribs, the fattiest section of the animal, and that single measurement grades the entire carcass, so every cut from that animal is sold under it,” she says. Since the grade measures taste, rather than nutrition or lifestyle conditions, leaner grass-fed and pasture-raised options may be graded lower simply for the lower fat content. Given that, she suggests looking at those kinds of meat, along with USDA Organic meat, if you’re more concerned with nutrition and animal welfare. “The best steak is the one that matches your goal,” she says.
The USDA grades meat into Prime, Choice and Select categories, with Prime being the highest, says Kais.

Meat delivery services are great for anyone, but especially for those looking to conveniently access cuts that they may not be able to find in their local grocery store. Plus, the delivery aspect makes it easier to plan your shopping, so your fridge is never empty. “Delivery guarantees it never runs out, at a quality you chose yourself,” says Pierrel.

How I picked the best hair sunscreens

Experts agree that you should be protecting both your scalp and hair. For your scalp, choose a broad-spectrum SPF 30 or higher in sprays, lightweight lotions, sticks and brush-on mineral powders, depending on your hairstyle and hair density. For the hair shaft, look for lightweight leave-in UV protectants that help prevent damage, moisture loss and color fading without making your hair greasy, says Dr. Kseniya Kobets, director of cosmetic dermatology at Montefiore Einstein Advanced Care Cosmetic Dermatology Center.
When shopping for a hair SPF, the dermatologists I spoke to recommend considering the following factors:

Broad-spectrum protection: Look for UV-protectant sprays or mists that clearly state “broad-spectrum protection” on the label. “These products create a protective barrier on the hair shaft and help reflect UV radiation away from the strands,” says board-certified cosmetic dermatologist Dr. Michele Green.Consistency: Choose a lightweight, non-greasy formula that won’t weigh your hair down or leave any residue. “Heavier sunscreen products designed for the skin can make hair appear oily or feel sticky. UV-filtering sprays and mists are best because they distribute evenly without disrupting your hairstyle,” says Green. Additionally, powder sunscreens with SPF can protect the scalp along the part line without adding any oil.Nourishing ingredients: Consider leave-in treatments that combine UV filters with nourishing ingredients like antioxidants or plant oils. “You’ll get both protection and added hydration in one convenient step,” says Green.

Consistency: Choose a lightweight, non-greasy formula that won’t weigh your hair down or leave any residue. “Heavier sunscreen products designed for the skin can make hair appear oily or feel sticky. UV-filtering sprays and mists are best because they distribute evenly without disrupting your hairstyle,” says Green. Additionally, powder sunscreens with SPF can protect the scalp along the part line without adding any oil.

Nourishing ingredients: Consider leave-in treatments that combine UV filters with nourishing ingredients like antioxidants or plant oils. “You’ll get both protection and added hydration in one convenient step,” says Green.
Do you need sunscreen for your hair?

Unlike your scalp, which needs SPF because you’re protecting skin from sunburn, premature aging and skin cancer, the hair shaft benefits from UV protection primarily for cosmetic reasons. Hair is made of keratin, which UV rays can damage over time, similar to how sun exposure breaks down collagen in the skin and leaves it weaker, says Green. The sun can strip your hair of its natural oils, fade its color and make it more susceptible to breakage and split ends. “This is particularly important for individuals with color-treated, chemically processed, or already damaged hair, as these types tend to be more porous and therefore more vulnerable to UV-related harm,” says Green.

Hair UV protectants, sometimes called Hair Protection Factor, help preserve color, strength, shine and smoothness. These are usually hair products, like leave-in conditioners, with built-in UV filters. “They’re especially helpful if you spend a lot of time outdoors or swim frequently,” says Kobets.

However, experts agree that physical protection, like wearing a wide-brimmed hat or wrapping your head in a scarf, can be more beneficial than a product with UV protection because they shield both your hair and scalp from direct sun exposure.
Frequently asked questions

Just like the skin on the rest of your body, your scalp is at risk of damage from the sun. “It can burn, age prematurely, develop precancerous lesions and increase your risk of skin cancer just like the rest of your body,” says Kobets. “This is especially important if you have thinning hair, part your hair down the middle, have a visible part or are bald.”

As for your hair shaft, the sun breaks down keratin, dries it out (UVB damage) and breaks down the color (UVA damage), says double board-certified facial plastic and reconstructive surgeon Dr. Jamie DeRosa. Sun damage can cause your hair to look dry, brittle and straw-like.

While you can spray or apply your favorite sunscreen onto your scalp, be prepared for your hair to look greasy and matted, says Evans. Traditional sunscreens are designed to sit on your skin and usually have heavier oils, waxes or thick emollients, which can make your hair look greasy, weighed down or coated with residue, says Green. They also don’t wash out easily, which can lead to buildup on your scalp, clogged hair follicles or irritation.
Instead, apply traditional sunscreen along your exposed hairline or on parts of the ears and neck that aren’t covered by hair, which are areas that still require standard SPF protection, says Green.

For an additional layer of protection, consider wearing UV-protective clothing (called UPF clothing), such as a wide-brimmed hat or wrapping your hair in a scarf. You can also use an umbrella to shield your hair from direct sun exposure and stay out of the sun during the highest UV times of the day (10 a.m. to midafternoon), says DeRosa.

title: How to prevent boob sweat, according to experts
summary: Beyond making you uncomfortable, boob sweat can cause painful sweat rashes under the breasts. Experts share the best boob sweat solutions and how to treat intertrigo.
story: Every time I experience boob sweat, I think one thing: There has to be a way to prevent this. That damp, gross feeling lingers for the rest of the day, and it’s even more miserable when it leads to painful rashes. Unfortunately, the experts I talked to say you can’t completely prevent boob sweat — it’s almost inevitable when heat and moisture get trapped under the breasts, and it’s especially common during hormonal changes like those that happen during menstruation, perimenopause, menopause and pregnancy. But there are ways to reduce boob sweat and avoid related skin irritation to keep you more comfortable.
Below, I talked to board-certified nurse practitioners about the most effective boob solutions, and how to treat sweat rashes under the breasts if you get them.

What causes boob sweat?

Boob sweat is caused by heat and moisture getting trapped in the skin fold between each breast and the chest, a.k.a. the underboob area. It’s a warm, closed-off  part of the body where heat and moisture can’t evaporate, so sweat easily builds up, says Madeline June, a board-certified nurse practitioner at The Well Westlake. Boob sweat can lead to uncomfortable rashes from chafing (irritation that happens when skin rubs on skin or clothing), or yeast and fungal overgrowth.

Experts told me that several factors exacerbate boob sweat, including high temperatures and humidity levels; hormonal changes, like those that happen during menstruation, pregnancy, perimenopause and menopause; and tight-fitting bras and clothes made from non-breathable fabric.
Can you prevent boob sweat?

No, you can’t completely prevent boob sweat, just like how you can’t completely prevent sweat on any part of your body. “It’s a common issue, not a hygiene failure, and most people experience it at some point,” says Courtney Coons, a board-certified nurse practitioner at PERK Plastic Surgery.
That said, you can use certain products and practice habits that help reduce boob sweat and prevent related skin irritation.

She recommends looking for one that’s non-constricting and made from moisture-wicking, breathable fabrics that reduce the chance of chafing.

How I picked the best boob sweat solutions

To pick the best boob sweat solutions, I talked to two board-certified nurse practitioners about products that absorb and reduce moisture on skin, and/or help prevent related skin irritation from occurring. Frequently asked questions
Some people are more prone to boob sweat than others, says June, including:

Those with larger breasts, which cause more skin-to-skin contact between the breasts and the chest, increasing how much heat and moisture gets trappedThose experiencing hormonal changes during menstruation, pregnancy, perimenopause and menopause, which can cause increased sweat production

Yes, boob sweat can cause rashes. They’re technically called intertrigo, a type of rash that develops in skin folds, like the ones between the breasts and the chest, says June.
There’s two types of boob sweat rashes to know about:

Heat rashes: When heat stays trapped in the skin fold, it often leads to chafing, which shows up as a raw, irritated rash from the constant friction, says Coons. Moisture rashes: When moisture stays trapped in the skin fold, it can lead to yeast or fungal overgrowth, which shows up as a red, itchy rash, says Coons.

Moisture rashes: When moisture stays trapped in the skin fold, it can lead to yeast or fungal overgrowth, which shows up as a red, itchy rash, says Coons.

To treat rashes from boob sweat, keep the affected area clean, dry and friction-free, says June. Also apply a barrier ointment like petroleum jelly (including Vaseline and Aquaphor) or a zinc oxide cream like Desitin to protect the skin. Topical steroids like hydrocortisone cream can help with itching and inflammation. By following this treatment plan, rashes usually heal within a few days of following this regime, says Coons.

If you don’t treat a rash right away, the irritated, inflamed skin can break down further, leading to open wounds that are more prone to infection, says Coons. Then, when those wounds heal, they can leave behind long-term skin discoloration — hyperpigmentation shows up as dark spots, while hypopigmentation shows us as light spots, says June.

It’s also important to know when to see a doctor about these rashes. Typical irritation presents as mild redness, itching or burning, and the skin is intact without drainage (clear fluid that leaks out of wounds), says June. If your rash isn’t getting better after a week of consistent at-home care, or it’s getting worse and you notice any of the following symptoms, it’s time to see a doctor as you could have an infection, says Coons: persistent redness, spreading redness, warmth, severe itching or burning, open sores with drainage, pain or odor. Your doctor can give you a prescription-strength treatment.
